CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right heel pain, at the back of the heel, in the setting of triathlon training.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Dennis is a new patient who is training for a triathlon. He reports pain in the back of the heel, mainly on the right, that typically occurs after a workout or when he first gets up in the morning. The pain extends from the back of the heel up into the calf. On first getting out of bed the area feels very tight, "almost like it's tearing." After walking for about 10 to 15 minutes it eases somewhat. It becomes sore again when he sits for an extended period and then gets up, and after a lot of activity. The left leg is not affected.

Training: he runs about 10 km in the morning, bikes 45 minutes to 1 hour at lunchtime, and swims 30 minutes to 1 hour in the evening. He does this five days a week. On weekends he alternates between a long run and a long bike and does not do a long swim. He takes one day off. He does not stretch at all because he has no time. On the bike he goes slowly at first until warmed up. Medication use was not asked about by the doctor, who assumed that whatever the patient had been doing was not working significantly. Early in the visit, before taking the history, the doctor said he thought it could be plantar fasciitis.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right heel and calf pain and tightness as described in the HPI. No left leg pain.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lower extremities, right side:
- Pulling toes up toward him (dorsiflexion) causes a little pain.
- Pushing against the doctor's resistance causes a little pain.
- Calf squeeze: no pain on either the left or right side. The doctor stated the Thompson test is negative.
- Squeezing the heel causes significant pain.
- Palpation up the Achilles tendon: very tender.

RESULTS
No imaging or laboratory results. The doctor sees no reason for an x-ray at this point.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Achilles tendinitis of the right side, from overuse in the setting of aggressive training for an event, per the doctor. Thompson test negative.

Plan:
1. Stop training for one to two weeks to allow healing.
2. Ibuprofen (Advil), three tablets every six hours, as an anti-inflammatory to reduce inflammation around the Achilles tendon.
3. Physical therapy referral for a couple of visits for strengthening and stretching education, including learning how to stretch the muscles before activity.
4. Follow-up in 7 to 10 days after the first couple of physical therapy appointments to monitor progress. The patient will call the office once physical therapy is scheduled.
5. No x-ray at this point. If he still has significant pain without change about ten days in, despite modified activity, the doctor said more aggressive treatment plans may need to be considered.

The patient agreed with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up of chronic problems: depression, hypertension, and status post rotator cuff repair.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Edward is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history significant for depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair who presents for follow-up of his chronic problems. His last visit was about six months ago. He reports the past six months have been good.

Depression: At the last visit he was working on new strategies to manage his depression and did not want to start medication because he is already on multiple medications. He now sees a counselor once a week and has been swimming at the pool frequently this summer and fall. He reports his depression is going well. He does not feel the need to start medication at this time and knows he can call if that changes.

Hypertension: He was struggling with blood pressure control six months ago. He reports he still has good days and bad days. He takes his medicine daily (Norvasc). He admits that burgers, wine, and salt occasionally sneak into his diet. He checks his blood pressure about once a week at a machine at CVS pharmacy.

Rotator cuff repair: The repair was done about eight months ago. He reports it is doing well. He has been stretching with a yoga ball and is getting stronger each time. He has progressed from physical therapy to home exercises and can continue them once a week.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Doing well overall.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain. Reports mild ankle swelling, mainly near the end of the day, that resolves by the next morning.
HEENT: Denies nasal congestion.
Psychiatric: Depression reported as well managed.
Musculoskeletal: Shoulder doing well, getting stronger.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 156/94, elevated. Home/recorded readings have been running a little high over the past couple of months.
Cardiovascular: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously heard in the past and appears stable to the doctor.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Lower extremities: 1 to 2+ pitting edema in the legs.
Doctor noted the remainder of the exam looked good.

RESULTS
Labs: Reviewed by the doctor as looking really good. Creatinine (kidney function) is stable.
EKG: Normal per the doctor, with no evidence of coronary artery disease.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: The doctor feels the patient is managing it well, with good strategies and a good support system. The doctor agrees no medication is needed at this time. Patient may call if this changes.

2. Hypertension: The doctor does not believe it is well controlled. Plan is to increase Norvasc to 10 mg daily and order an echocardiogram and a lipid panel.

3. Leg edema: Pitting edema on exam and patient-reported ankle swelling in the evenings. In the visit, the doctor said it might be poor circulation but was unsure, and also said it may be related to salt intake. Plan is to discuss diet and decreasing salt intake.

4. Status post rotator cuff repair: The doctor feels the patient is doing really well and the problem is pretty much resolved. Continue home exercises. No further intervention is needed.

The patient had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up visit for diabetes. Also discussed hypertension, high cholesterol, vascular disease of the legs, foot symptoms, and smoking.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Maria Martin, date of birth 03/05/1946, consented to recording of the visit. She reports feeling "pretty good," about the same as before.

Diabetes: The doctor's letter after the last visit reported poorly controlled sugars, with an A1c of 9.9. The letter instructed her to increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice a day. She did not increase it and is still taking 2 mg. She recently filled the prescription. Diet: she does not eat pasta and does not keep it at home. She rarely has bread, and buys wheat bread when she does. She usually has two slices in the morning and occasionally a peanut butter sandwich. She hardly drinks sodas and drinks club soda or seltzer instead of regular water. The doctor advised cutting down the number of bread slices per day. She is also on metformin.

Eyes: She reports eye exams are up to date and she recently got new glasses. She goes to the optometry group on Liberty Road, where the doctor changes each visit. She previously saw Dr. Sanchez, from whom she recently got her prescription. She had cataract surgery, followed by a month of healing before the prescription was written. She is not happy with the lens in one eye, which she says is "kinda funny"; the other eye is good.

Hypertension: She reports a home blood pressure of 116 a couple of weeks ago. She reports taking metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril-hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg daily, and amlodipine 10 mg daily.

Cholesterol and leg vascular disease: She is on atorvastatin and reports tolerating it. She states her feet "feel like hell" all the time and her legs bother her. She cannot do much walking. She says it might be sciatica but is not sure. She also reports pain up to the hip, in the hips and upper legs. The doctor said the feet are, in his opinion, peripheral neuropathy, and that these symptoms seem relatively stable. She is trying to walk.

Tobacco: She is still smoking and is not ready to quit. She says she will think about it.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Neurologic: No headaches or dizziness. Feels "totally normal" in this regard. Reports foot and leg discomfort, as above.
Eyes: Vision improved after cataract surgery, but she is not happy with the lens in one eye.
Respiratory: Recent cough with congestion; sputum is relatively clear. Cough was better this morning. No shortness of breath.
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, pressure, or tightness.
GI: No nausea, vomiting, or GI symptoms.
GU: Slower urinary stream, which she describes as stable and attributes to age. Urinates several times per day. Nocturia only once in a while. She tends to drink in the evening.
Musculoskeletal: Pain in the hips and upper legs, as above.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Carotids normal, no bruits.
Cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, normal rate, S1 and S2 crisp, no murmurs.
Lungs: Clear, no rales or wheezing.
Extremities: No edema. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable. Thickened nails. Mildly dry skin, no skin breakdown. Monofilament sensation mildly decreased at the tips of the first and second toes.
Blood pressure rechecked in clinic: 140/60.

RESULTS
Previous A1c was 9.9 (per the doctor, average blood sugar above 9). No new results today.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Type 2 diabetes, poorly controlled: A1c 9.9 at last check. Increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice a day. Until the new prescription is picked up, she is to take two of her 2 mg tablets twice a day. The new prescription is for 4 mg tablets, one tablet twice a day. Continue metformin. Counseled to watch for low sugars (weak, shaky, sweaty) and to call if they occur; the doctor does not expect this. Recheck labs today. Dietary advice: cut down the number of bread slices per day.
2. Hypertension: Clinic BP 140/60, and home readings are better. Continue the current combination of medications (metoprolol, lisinopril-hydrochlorothiazide, amlodipine). Check kidney function today.
3. Hyperlipidemia and peripheral vascular disease: Continue high-dose atorvastatin to protect the arteries.
4. Peripheral neuropathy of the feet (the doctor's impression): Mildly decreased sensation on exam. Keep feet moisturized. A medication is available if symptoms become really bad, but she is already on many medications. She may buy a foot scrub or cream to use after showers.
5. Cataract surgery with dissatisfaction with one lens: The doctor noted that the eye can sometimes be cleaned up with laser, but will see what the eye doctors say.
6. Tobacco use: The doctor advised quitting. She is not ready but will think about it.
7. Everything else unchanged. Labs today. Return in four months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after an emergency room visit for shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Louis is a 58-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure who presents for follow-up after an ER visit. On Saturday he was playing tennis in very hot, humid weather. After about half an hour he became very short of breath and struggled to breathe. He thought he was having a heart attack. His wife took him to the ER, where "everything checked out." The doctor wondered whether this might have been heat exhaustion. About six hours after returning home, he felt very lightheaded and dizzy. On Sunday he felt fine. He came in because he thought a check-up was worthwhile.

He reports being very diligent with his heart failure medications and is in touch with his doctor. He tries to avoid junk food and salty foods but admits to "cheating" every now and then; for the most part he has done well.

Cataract removal was done three months ago, and he has had no vision problems since. Skin cancer was removed about five months ago; it healed nicely with no problems since.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Shortness of breath during tennis on Saturday, as above.
Neurological: Lightheadedness and dizziness about six hours after returning home from the ER; resolved by Sunday.
Eyes: No vision problems.
Skin: No problems at the skin cancer removal site.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure a little high. The doctor noted that the ER report also showed high blood pressure.
Neck: Very supple. No jugular venous distention appreciated.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur.
Respiratory: Fine crackles bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema in both legs.

RESULTS
ECG: Stable for the patient. Shows left ventricular hypertrophy, which the doctor stated caused his congestive heart failure.
Echocardiogram: Pumping function of the heart is a little low but stable.
Skin biopsy pathology: Doctor's review indicates all of the skin cancer was removed and everything is fine.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Shortness of breath, likely heart failure exacerbation: The doctor's impression is that this was an exacerbation of congestive heart failure, with probable dietary indiscretion (salty food) causing fluid retention. Exam findings of fine bibasilar crackles and trace leg edema were interpreted by the doctor as possible extra fluid on board. Heat exhaustion was raised earlier by the doctor as a possibility. Plan: prescribe an extra dose of Lasix 80 mg once daily and start carvedilol 25 mg twice daily. Both were ordered.
2. Elevated blood pressure: Elevated today and in the ER. The doctor said it will need to be discussed; no specific plan was made.
3. Congestive heart failure: Echocardiogram shows stable, mildly reduced pumping function. The doctor noted he is on appropriate medication therapy.
4. Status post cataract surgery and skin cancer removal: Doing well. No medication adjustments needed.
The nurse will see the patient shortly.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lower back pain after an injury about four months ago.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jeremy injured his lower back about four months ago while moving boxes during his son's move out of a college dorm. He thinks it might be a pulled muscle but is not sure. He delayed being seen because appointments were backed up. He tried physical therapy at his gym, which did not seem to help, and he became concerned.

At the time of injury, for a very short period it felt like he was going to topple over and could not support his upper body weight. The toes on his right foot also tingled a little, which resolved after about an hour. The numbness and tingling occurred only when he first felt the "tweak" in his back and has not recurred. He has leg weakness only when carrying something heavy, otherwise his legs feel relatively normal. He is nervous about carrying heavy objects. He still has sharp pain in the lower back when he turns a certain way or rolls over in his sleep, which wakes him; it resolves when he repositions.

He has taken Tylenol and ibuprofen and has tried heat and ice, with nothing helping much. Ibuprofen is a little better than Tylenol but works for a shorter time. He has had no stomach upset from ibuprofen, and he tries not to take too much. He went to urgent care, where an MRI was recommended. He did not get it because of concern that insurance was maxed out and because he started to feel better. Because symptoms have gone on so long, he now wants to proceed with the MRI. He denies bladder or bowel problems, incontinence, or inability to urinate or defecate. He denies fever or chills.

Past medical history: right total knee replacement in spring 2020 (about two years ago). He rehabbed with PT, and the knee feels about 95 percent normal.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Musculoskeletal: Lower back pain with certain movements; intermittent leg weakness with heavy carrying.
Neurological: Transient right toe tingling at injury, resolved; no current numbness or tingling.
Genitourinary/Gastrointestinal: No incontinence or difficulty with urination or bowel movements; no stomach upset with ibuprofen.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: No temperature elevation noted, blood pressure about 117/56, heart rate 68, oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
Neck: Bony protuberance of C5-C6 appreciated; no pain to palpation.
Lumbar spine: No pain to palpation. Decreased flexion and extension of the lower back. Positive straight leg raise. Spasm of the paraspinal muscles of the lumbar spine.
Musculoskeletal: Lower extremity strength equal bilaterally.

RESULTS
Lumbar spine x-ray: No acute bony abnormality and no fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
The doctor believes Jeremy has an acute disc herniation, based on his ongoing symptoms even though the injury occurred a few months ago. The doctor said the exam findings may reflect some arthritis in the neck and/or a minor injury from the back event, and that overall things look good.

Plan:
1. Order a lumbar spine MRI for a better look at soft tissue, since x-rays show only bone.
2. Continue physical therapy; refer to a physical therapist through the health system.
3. Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once daily.
4. If a herniated disc is confirmed, other options such as an epidural steroid injection could be discussed to reduce inflammation. The doctor said it might help him feel better, to be addressed if the time comes.

The patient had no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Elevated and fluctuating blood pressure readings.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
67-year-old male with history of essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. Blood pressure is normally very well controlled. Over the last 3 to 4 weeks he has had periods of lightheadedness and slight headache. When he checked his blood pressure, the systolic has occasionally been over 180, higher than any prior readings. He has checked it both when feeling fine and during lightheaded episodes, and readings during the lightheaded episodes have been on the high side. He describes the dizziness as feeling "fuzzy" and lightheaded, not spinning. He feels a little unsteady when dizzy. He has had a slight headache when blood pressure is higher. He has not passed out recently. He reports occasional mild chest heaviness, nothing sustained. No breathing difficulty. No fever, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Palpitations are not usual.

Medications: lisinopril 20 mg twice daily (increased from once daily at last visit); he reports rarely missing doses. He uses a pillbox and has tried a medication reminder app, which he found a bit confusing, but says he is staying on his schedule accurately. He continues atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia. For osteoarthritis, he is mostly able to golf and walk the course, but when the weather changes he sometimes plays less or skips a day. He takes Tylenol for mild pain and adjusts activity as needed.

The doctor wondered early in the visit whether an inner ear problem might be involved; this was a passing comment and was not pursued or confirmed.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever.
Cardiovascular: Occasional mild chest heaviness, not sustained. No palpitations usually. No recent syncope.
Respiratory: No breathing difficulty.
GI: No nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Neurologic: Lightheadedness ("fuzzy"), slight unsteadiness with dizziness, slight headache with higher blood pressure. No spinning sensation.
Musculoskeletal: Mild osteoarthritis pain managed with Tylenol, worse with weather changes.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiac: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior.
Lungs: Mild bibasilar rales, no wheezes or rhonchi, excellent air movement.
Extremities: Trace bilateral lower extremity edema.
Otherwise, exam described as normal and unremarkable.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Elevated blood pressure (history of essential hypertension): The doctor assessed that blood pressure is somewhat out of control and needs adjustment.
- Increase lisinopril to 60 mg twice daily (as stated in the transcript).
- Add hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.
- Check blood pressure twice daily for the next 2 weeks.
- Follow up in 2 weeks.
- Stay well hydrated, 6 to 8 glasses of water per day, more if dehydrated or more active in warm weather.
- Limit alcohol (beer) to no more than a couple of drinks per week given fluctuating blood pressure.

2. Hyperlipidemia:
- Continue atorvastatin.
- Order cholesterol panel, CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis (to look at kidney function).

3. Osteoarthritis:
- Continue to stay active without overdoing it, including walking and golfing.
- Tylenol as needed for mild pain.

4. Heart murmur: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur unchanged from prior; the doctor is not concerned and is continuing to monitor.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chronic back pain for about two years.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Steven reports back pain for about a couple of years. He attributes the onset to a fall on his back while playing basketball and says the pain has persisted since then. He thinks it could be arthritis. He rates the pain about 7/10. It is sharp and sometimes throbbing, and it is sometimes worse than at other times for reasons he is not sure of. It radiates down his left leg, and his toes sometimes get a little numb. He reports sometimes feeling weak when trying to stand up or after standing for too long. Lying on his side improves the pain, and standing for a while worsens it. When asked about loss of sensation in the genital or rectal area, he responded "I hope not" and did not clearly answer. He reports one episode of bowel incontinence over the two years, which was not consistent. He thinks it may have been related to standing too long and possibly drinking.

Prior treatments: a doctor gave injections in the past, and he does not know what they were. He said he needed to be held down for them because he dislikes needles. Physical therapy was not very helpful. He felt he could do the same exercises at home, though he said it helped "a little." He took a white pill for pain, name unknown, and later said it worked. The doctor noted in the chart that he had been given strong pain medications.

Currently he is sedentary, sitting at home and watching TV. He reports gaining about 80 pounds in the past year. Family history: a fourth cousin has scoliosis, and he does not think any direct relatives have spine conditions. He initially was reluctant but acknowledged having smoked in the past. He declined to give details and said he does not currently smoke.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Chronic back pain, leg weakness at times with standing.
Neurological: Intermittent numbness in the toes, pain radiating down the left leg. Did not clearly answer the question about genital or rectal sensory loss.
GI: One episode of bowel incontinence.
Constitutional: Weight gain of about 80 pounds in the past year.
Psychiatric: Anxiety and dislike of needles regarding injections.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: The doctor reviewed vitals and stated that something appears to be in the 95th percentile range, which may need exploration. The specific parameter was not stated.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur appreciated.
Back: No overlying erythema or ecchymosis. Midline tenderness at the L4-L5 disc space with right-sided lumbar paravertebral tenderness. Pain with lumbar flexion and, to a lesser degree, extension. Supine straight leg raise positive.
Neurological: Decreased sensation to light touch at the right lateral thigh (L4 dermatome). Patellar and Achilles reflexes symmetric.

RESULTS
MRI: Disc desiccation, disc bulge with paracentral disc herniation resulting in moderate right neural foraminal stenosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Chronic lumbar back pain, consistent with L4-L5 herniated disc with radiculopathy, per the doctor based on symptoms, exam, and MRI. The doctor explained that the disc is bulging and pinching nerves, which explains the leg symptoms and the tenderness on exam.
- Recommend spinal corticosteroid injection under fluoroscopy. The procedure is quick and common, takes about an hour, and if successful would be done at most about four times a year.
- The patient dislikes needles. The doctor will prescribe an anti-anxiety medication to take about three hours before the procedure.
- The patient asked for pain pills. The doctor said pain medication should not be needed after the injection. If pain persists about a day after the injection, pain medication can be discussed. The doctor does not want him on long-term pain medication.
- If pain persists after monitoring, the doctor said surgery might be recommended. The patient said he does not want surgery. The doctor plans to try all other options first.
- The patient will schedule the injection at the front desk. He had no further questions.

2. Smoking history and elevated vital sign percentile: the doctor said these may need further exploration. The doctor commented that smoking likely has a stronger impact than weight gain. No specific plan was stated.

Home blood pressure: She checks at home. Morning readings are lower and generally in the expected range. Evening readings run about 130-145/150 over 95-100 diastolic. She acknowledges that she would need to stop drinking for her blood pressure to be okay. She asked about the shot mentioned at the last visit. She has taken similar medications in the past and believes she has probably tried naltrexone in pill form. She says she would not take a daily pill but would accept a shot.

She denies chest tightness or pressure and shortness of breath. She denies fever, cough, and sore throat. She denies recent travel and known exposure to coronavirus. She received her coronavirus vaccine on February 9th.

Constitutional: No fever. Earlier fatigue/lethargy after the first full dose of lisinopril, which improved on a half dose.

Right ankle injury after a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jaqueline is a patient who fell off her bike during a mountain biking lesson and injured her right ankle. She reports the ankle twisted outward. Pain is greatest at the outer (lateral) ankle. She can move the ankle only a little and is not really able to walk on it. She is limping. She heard a crack or crackle at the time of injury. She took Tylenol, which did not help. The patient wondered whether this might be an Achilles tendon tear. She has been mountain biking for about three years.

Regarding numbness and tingling, her answers were inconsistent: she said she had some tingling, then no tingling, and some numbness "in other places," specifying her heart. The doctor noted he is an orthopedic physician and could not address this. Numbness or tingling in the toes was not clearly confirmed.

She reported a fever "when the pain hits," with a value of "like two hundred," which the doctor said is not a fever.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Patient reported fever when the pain hits, with a stated value of "two hundred," which is not a plausible temperature. Temperature in the office was normal.
Musculoskeletal: Right ankle pain, decreased ability to move the ankle, difficulty walking, limping.
Neurological: Inconsistent report of tingling and numbness; numbness described in "other places" including the heart. Toe numbness or tingling was not clearly confirmed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Temperature 98.6, blood pressure 118/77, heart rate 77 beats per minute.
Right ankle: Edema and erythema over the lateral malleolus, with associated ecchymosis and a few excoriations. Pain to palpation of the right lateral malleolus. Decreased flexion and extension, and decreased internal and external rotation. No apparent injury to the knee or foot.

RESULTS
Right ankle x-ray (obtained by the nurse before the visit and reviewed by the doctor): No acute fracture or bony abnormality. Findings consistent with soft tissue injury per the doctor.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Acute right ankle sprain (doctor's assessment). The patient's own concern was a possible Achilles tendon tear; the doctor did not diagnose this.
- Air cast.
- Crutches.
- Meloxicam 15 mg once daily.
- Ice for about 20 minutes, five times a day.
- Weight-bear as tolerated.
- The doctor anticipates improvement in the next couple of weeks. If not improving, return to clinic to consider physical therapy or further imaging.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right hip pain in the groin area.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ms. Reyes is a 56-year-old woman with right groin pain since February 2020. She wonders whether it might be a hernia (patient's own speculation). The pain began while she was walking around the infusion room, initially when she took a step back, and now occurs with any movement. It hurts when she pivots. The hip catches and grabs, and she almost falls. Sometimes she does fall. Episodes are unpredictable: sometimes a movement triggers it and sometimes it does not, and sometimes it happens several times in a row. Pain ranges from 2 to 7 out of 10. She feels better when she stays still but does not want to stay still. She denies fever, chills, tingling, numbness, and bowel or bladder problems.

Past medical history: multiple surgeries, including PCL surgery, infertility, and gallbladder removal. She reports several bulging discs in the back, but the weight loss has greatly decreased that pain. She has had intentional weight loss of 110 pounds with Weight Watchers, started in 2018, and has been at her current weight a little over a year.
Family history: high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, heart disease, kidney disease, and gastric ulcers.
Medications: none currently.
Allergies: Percocet, Vicodin, and "regulin" (as transcribed).
Social history: works at an infusion center, lives with a roommate, no tobacco, and limits alcohol to fewer than five drinks per month.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills. Intentional weight loss as above.
Musculoskeletal: Right groin/hip pain with catching and falls. No back pain currently.
Neurological: No tingling or numbness.
GI/GU: No bowel or bladder problems.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant 56-year-old woman, 5 feet 6 inches, 169 pounds.
Vitals: Blood pressure 115/75, pulse 67.
Extremities: No ankle edema, no calf tenderness.
Gait: Heel walk and toe walk intact.
Cervical spine: No tenderness. Full range of motion without pain. Spurling's test negative.
Low back: Skin intact, no midline tenderness to palpation. No pain with extension, lateral bending, or forward flexion. Range of motion decreased on exertion per dictation. Lateral flexion without pain. Sacroiliac signs negative.
Hips: Trochanteric region non-tender. Range of motion decreased in the right hip, with groin pain on internal and external rotation. Resisted right hip flexion causes pain in the right groin region. Mild pain with knee lift on the patient's report.
Neurological: Motor control normal in the lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes 1+ throughout. No focal motor weakness. No focal sensory deficit. Sensation to touch intact.

RESULTS
Radiographs and MR arthrogram of the right hip, done June 3, 2021: high-grade chondromalacia involving the anterosuperior right acetabulum (dictated as "interosuperior") with subchondral marrow edema and cyst formation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right hip degenerative joint disease (doctor's impression).
Options discussed:
- Low-impact exercise program, with a handout of exercises.
- NSAIDs as needed for pain and discomfort.
- Cane to offload the right side. The patient does not love the idea but will try it.
- Cortisone injection into the right hip joint. The patient definitely wants it.
The injection will be given today. The doctor explained the risks, the patient reviewed them, understood, and consented. Follow up in three months to assess progress, with another injection if needed.

The doctor also asked that the surgical list be included in the note. The only surgeries the patient named are listed above under past medical history.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Bilateral knee pain for about six months, referred by primary care physician.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Sophia presents with approximately six months of knee pain. She cannot recall any specific event or injury that triggered it. She describes a deep, achy pain behind the kneecaps, with occasional creaking in the knees. The patient herself wondered whether it might be tendonitis but said she was not sure.

Pain is worse when going from sitting to standing, such as after sitting at her desk (she works from home) or after watching TV, and with going up and down stairs. Resting for some time helps the pain.

Treatments tried: ice and an Ace bandage wrap when the pain first started. She takes ibuprofen or Aleve sometimes but tries to avoid medications.

She is active and loves to run outdoors, using a treadmill in winter. She previously ran five to six miles per day but now cannot get to half a mile before her knee starts hurting.

She denies noticeable swelling or redness of the knees. No prior knee injuries. She has never broken a bone other than her arm in sixth grade.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Bilateral knee pain with creaking as above. No knee swelling or redness.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Reviewed by the doctor, who said they overall look good (no values stated).
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs.
Musculoskeletal: Normal gait. Strength 3/5 for bilateral leg abduction; remaining lower extremity strength 5/5.
Knees: No overlying erythema, ecchymosis, or warmth of the skin. No effusion. Tenderness to palpation of the bilateral retinaculum. Positive patellar grind test. Squatting is possible but painful. Lachman, anterior and posterior drawer, and McMurray tests negative bilaterally.
Neuro: Patellar and Achilles reflexes symmetric.

RESULTS
Knee X-rays (both knees), reviewed by the doctor: no fractures or osteoarthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Bilateral knee pain. Based on the history, exam, and imaging review, the doctor stated the symptoms are consistent with patellofemoral pain syndrome, a common condition especially in active young people, related to how the patella tracks along the groove of the femur. (The doctor referred to reviewing an MRI during the assessment, but only X-ray results were described earlier.)

Plan:
- May continue ibuprofen or another anti-inflammatory as needed for pain.
- Physical therapy recommended for lower extremity exercises to increase strength and mobility and to correct any incorrect running mechanics.
- Take it easy from running for now. Returning to running is a goal of treatment. Progress will be assessed at each visit.
- Doctor will follow up with the patient soon.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left arm pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Donald Clark, DOB 03/04/1937, is an elderly man referred by another physician (the patient did not recall her name; the doctor referred to her as Betty) for left arm pain. Symptoms began about two weeks ago. He woke around 2:00 AM with severe pain in the arm and hand. Ice eased it. Sitting at the bedside and holding the arm down, thinking it would help circulation, did not help. Pain eased around 4-5 AM, and he went back to sleep without recurrence that night. This recurred over several nights. After the third episode he saw the referring physician, who told him it was most likely from a pinched nerve.

Pain starts in the hand and goes all the way down the arm. If it bothers him at night, it usually bothers him some the following day. Moving the neck or shoulder does not bother the arm. He reports hand weakness, including with gripping. He also reports an old finger injury; the finger does not work properly or works very rarely. The referring physician gave him numbing medicine, which helped a little, a "neck pill," and gabapentin. Since then it has not bothered him much at night. For the last couple of nights, and by his report for the last week, his neck has not bothered him, but his hand is still bothering him. He is unsure of his gabapentin dose; his lady friend helps manage his medications.

He is a veteran and has service-connected disability for leg issues from the knees to the feet, which he confirmed is neuropathy. The doctor initially wondered aloud whether this might be carpal tunnel syndrome, but this was not pursued further.

Anticoagulants: the patient first said he takes no blood thinners, then later stated he is taking Eliquis. This was not reconciled in the conversation. The doctor's dictated plan states he denies any blood thinners.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left arm and hand pain as above; no pain with neck or shoulder movement by history; a little neck strain with head turning during exam.
Neurologic: Hand weakness with gripping; chronic leg neuropathy; nonfunctioning finger after prior injury.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Elderly white man in a wheelchair, no apparent distress.
Neurologic: Reflexes 1+ bilateral biceps; triceps and brachioradialis reflexes also recorded as bilateral, negative. Strength and sensation per template for upper and lower extremities. Sensation felt the same in both hands on exam. Gait not assessed.
Musculoskeletal: Non-tender over the cervical spine. Mildly restricted cervical extension and right and left lateral rotation, symmetric, causing mild lateral neck pain but no radicular pain. Patient reported a little neck strain with range of motion. Spurling's maneuver benign. Grip squeeze and arm resistance testing performed.

RESULTS
Cervical x-ray: significant disc degeneration at C5-6, and to a lesser extent C4-5 and C3-4. Significant lower lumbar facet arthropathy was dictated (as written). C6-7 and C7-T1 are difficult to visualize. The doctor also noted a lot of arthritis in the neck and the potential for a disc pushing on a nerve. No cervical MRI is available; the patient has had a prior lumbar MRI.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Impression:
1. Left upper extremity neuropathy, suspicious for cervical radiculopathy, with possible contribution of peripheral neuropathy.
2. Neck pain in the setting of arthritis and disc degeneration.

The doctor agrees with the referring physician that the symptoms more than likely come from the neck, and suspects a flare of cervical radiculopathy. He suggested that the neck may go off-tilt during sleep and compress the nerve roots, and that the problem will likely flare up again.

Plan:
- Order cervical MRI to identify where the nerve roots are compressed. It cannot likely be done today; the doctor will talk with Roy to schedule it as soon as possible.
- Tentatively plan a left C7-T1 epidural steroid injection after the MRI, with the exact location pending MRI results. The doctor described it as a focused anti-inflammatory medicine placed behind the affected nerve roots. The patient agreed to proceed with the MRI and epidural rather than wait, since his hand still bothers him.
- Continue gabapentin twice daily (dose unclear to patient) and the home exercise program.
- Follow up after the epidural to assess relief.
- Anticoagulant status needs clarification given the patient's statement that he takes Eliquis.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right flank pain radiating to the groin for two weeks; suspected kidney stone.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient reports two weeks of pain that starts in the right flank and radiates down to the groin. The pain is intermittent and varies with how much he has been drinking and with his activities, but it never fully goes away. Most of the time it is 1-2 out of 10, and during flares it reaches about 4 out of 10. He had one episode in which the pain radiated to a testicle, and that has since calmed down. He denies pain with urination and denies blood in the urine. He denies nausea and vomiting. He felt he may have had chills but denies fevers. Ibuprofen calms the pain somewhat, but the pain persists. He saw his PCP before this visit and was given a urine strainer. He has been using it and has caught no stone so far.

He has a prior history of kidney stones. He has passed some on his own, usually within about a week, and has needed surgery a couple of times. Everyone in his family has had kidney stones.

At the start of the visit, the doctor wondered whether this might be a urinary tract infection.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Possible chills; no fevers.
GI: No nausea or vomiting.
GU: No dysuria, no hematuria. One episode of pain radiating to a testicle that has since calmed down.
Musculoskeletal/Pain: Right flank pain radiating to the groin.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure slightly elevated; the doctor thinks this is probably due to pain.
Abdomen: No tenderness to palpation.
Back: Right CVA tenderness, which the doctor attributes to the kidney stone.
Other: The doctor stated everything else looked fine.

RESULTS
CT scan: 0.5 cm stone in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right proximal ureteral kidney stone (0.5 cm) without hydronephrosis, in a patient with recurrent stones.
- The doctor hopes surgery will not be needed this time.
- Continue pushing fluids to try to pass the stone.
- Continue ibuprofen. The patient says it is working so far but would like something stronger for the weekend.
- Prescribe tramadol 50 mg for pain. Ibuprofen can be used for breakthrough pain.
- Continue straining urine with each void to catch the stone.
- Order BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture. Antibiotics will be considered based on results. The doctor does not think there is an infection, but it is possible.
- Follow up in 1-2 weeks (the doctor ended the visit saying "two weeks"). If symptoms persist and the stone has not passed, discuss further treatment, possibly lithotripsy. The patient has had lithotripsy before and says that is what he wants.
- The nurse will bring the tramadol prescription.
- The patient had no further questions.

note_text:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Annual exam.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Sarah is a 27-year-old female presenting for her annual visit.

Depression: She reports she has been doing better overall but has struggled off and on with depression, more so over the past year because she has been confined indoors and remote. She is taking Prozac 20 mg daily. She feels a lot has been weighing on her lately. The medication has helped in the past, and she thinks increasing the dose might help her through this patch. The doctor remarked that it might be vitamin D deficiency, but stated he was not sure.

Chronic back pain: She is managing it, but it remains intermittent. It bothers her when she sits for long periods at her desk at work; it gets stiff and hurts. It helps when she gets up and moves. She is also bothered by being on her feet too long, describing the extremes of each end. She reports a little numbness down her legs, described as almost like the legs falling asleep, but no tingling or pain down the legs. Symptoms improve with standing or changing position. No leg weakness. She is able to perform activities of daily living.

Cardiac history: She had a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) fairly young in life. She states she had a congenital artery problem as a baby. She reports her heart has been doing well and her arteries have been looking good.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Psychiatric: Depression symptoms off and on, as above.
Musculoskeletal: Chronic back pain and stiffness with prolonged sitting or standing, as above.
Neurologic: Mild leg numbness (feeling of falling asleep); no tingling, no leg pain, no leg weakness.
Cardiovascular: Reports her heart has been doing well.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: No apparent distress.
Neck: No thyroid enlargement.
Cardiovascular: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, stable.
Lungs: Clear.
Abdomen: Soft.
Musculoskeletal: Pain to palpation of the lumbar spine. Decreased flexion of the back.
Extremities: Lower extremity strength is good. No edema.

RESULTS
ECG: Basically unchanged from last year.
Lumbar spine x-ray: Looks good, stable from last year.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: Increase Prozac from 20 mg to 40 mg, one tablet once daily. Sent to her pharmacy. The patient agrees.
2. Chronic back pain: Physical therapy referral ordered. Pain medication was offered for periodic pain with activity, but the patient declined and prefers to start with physical therapy.
3. Status post CABG: Order repeat echocardiogram. Continue aspirin 81 mg daily.
4. The nurse will help schedule the referral and tests.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Lawrence is a 62-year-old male with a past medical history of type I diabetes (on an insulin pump), congestive heart failure, depression, and reflux who presents with shortness of breath.

He reports about 10 days of shortness of breath, noticeable when walking up a flight of stairs. He reports some leg swelling, feeling that he is "swelling up a little bit," and feeling very lethargic. He thinks this is largely related to attending house parties and eating salty foods. The doctor wondered whether it might be a kidney problem. He is a little uncomfortable and stiff when he wakes in the morning, and it takes a while to adjust to walking after getting up. He had one episode of waking acutely short of breath at night about a week ago, which has not recurred, and he has not been concerned about it.

Diabetes: He monitors his blood sugars well during the work week but forgets on Saturdays and Sundays because they are busy. He has not seen any spikes. He has an affinity for chocolate bars.

Depression: He describes a "crazy year and a half." He has tried natural approaches, including outdoor stretches every morning in the summer, which helped, but the weather has changed and he needs alternatives. He is not ready to try medications and is open to suggestions. He denies any thoughts of harming himself or others.

Reflux: He is on omeprazole and has been making lifestyle modifications, including cutting back on Red Bull and caffeine. Alcohol intake was tough during the holiday season, but he reports he is better.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for shortness of breath, leg swelling, lethargy, and morning stiffness. Denies chest pain, fever, chills, cough, and abdominal pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Look good per the doctor; pulse oximetry (oxygenation) looks good while sitting.
Neck: No jugular venous distension or carotid bruits.
Heart: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Lungs: Crackles bilaterally at the bases.
Lower extremities: 1+ pitting edema.

RESULTS
Chest x-ray: Reviewed by the doctor; looks good, with no evidence of airspace disease or pneumonia. The doctor noted this does not rule out fluid retention.
Labs: Look okay. White blood cell count is not elevated, so the doctor is not concerned about infection.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Shortness of breath, acute heart failure exacerbation: The doctor thinks he is retaining fluid, probably from dietary indiscretion.
- Start Lasix 40 mg daily.
- Weigh himself every day. Call the doctor if weight is not going down or is going up.
- If he becomes more short of breath at rest, call the doctor or 911 and go to the emergency room, where he might need intravenous diuretics.
- Call if any problems with breathing.

2. Type I diabetes:
- Order a hemoglobin A1c in about a month to see if adjustments are needed.
- Follow up with endocrinologist.
- Ensure a recent eye exam.

3. Depression:
- Refer to psychiatry for talk therapy.
- No medications.

4. Reflux:
- Continue omeprazole 20 mg daily.

The patient had no questions at this time.

Right upper leg pain after a bowling injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mrs. Peterson is a 43-year-old woman who presents with right upper leg pain. The doctor initially wondered whether it might be a pulled muscle. While bowling, she ran up to the lane with the ball all the way back and, on swinging it forward, hit the ball into her leg instead of the lane. She then fell and dropped the ball. She reports that the leg did not seem to swell much. She has a little bruising on the back side of the leg. She has been able to walk on it only a little, very carefully, and it is very sore to walk on. She does not have stairs at home but would avoid them at all costs. She has been alternating ibuprofen and Tylenol.

Past medical history: atopic eczema, for which she uses fluocinonide when it gets very itchy, with usual relief.
Past surgical history: colectomy (partial removal of colon) after diverticulosis progressed to diverticulitis.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right upper leg pain, soreness with walking, minor bruising posteriorly. Patient reports no significant swelling.
Skin: History of eczema, as above.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Musculoskeletal: Significant tenderness to the lateral aspect of the right upper leg, with pain on palpation. No pain with passive lifting of the leg. No pain or tenderness with flexion or extension of the lower leg.

RESULTS
Right femur x-ray (reviewed by the doctor): normal femur. No evidence of fracture or swelling. Essentially a normal x-ray.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right upper leg pain after a bowling injury. The doctor's impression is that she probably has a contusion; the x-ray shows no fracture.
- Start Mobic (meloxicam) 15 mg once daily as an anti-inflammatory.
- Use ice for pain.
- The doctor expects improvement within about a week, as is typical for a contusion.
- Return to clinic if not improving.
- Orders and procedures to be entered as described.

She denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or medication side effects from metformin.

The patient reports no one has told her about high blood pressure. She is not on any blood pressure medications. She asked whether high blood pressure could be causing her chest pain. The doctor said it could be contributing. The patient mentioned that someone had told her this before.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Numbness and tingling in the right hand.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Alexis is a patient who sits at a keyboard all day and reports numbness and tingling in the right hand. Symptoms have been present on and off for approximately six months and have become more persistent over the last month. Numbness and tingling are now constant. She has some pain, mostly while typing on the keyboard. Using her mouse also aggravates the pain. Not typing on the keyboard helps most, and she has been taking ibuprofen. Symptoms are mostly in the right hand. Numbness and symptoms are mainly in the thumb, index finger, and middle finger. Pain and tingling do not wake her at night and do not affect her sleep.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Neurological: Numbness and tingling in the right hand, mainly thumb, index, and middle fingers. No nighttime waking from pain or tingling.
Musculoskeletal: Right hand/wrist pain with typing and mouse use.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Right hand/wrist: Pain with wrist flexion and extension. Decreased grip strength on the right compared with expected. Tapping the inner wrist/forearm produced grimacing and shooting pain; the doctor documented a positive Tinel's sign. Sensory symptoms reported in the thumb, index, and middle fingers.

RESULTS
No test results available. EMG/nerve conduction study ordered (see plan).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Carpal tunnel syndrome, right hand, per the doctor's impression, based on history and exam. The doctor noted it is common in people who do data entry or repetitive tasks. The doctor explained that thickening of tissues in the wrist is compressing nerves. (The doctor initially remarked early in the visit that it might be a pinched nerve, uncertain at that time.)

Plan:
1. Wrist splint to be worn at night.
2. Continue ibuprofen, increasing to 600 mg four times a day.
3. Outpatient EMG/nerve conduction study of the wrist ordered.
4. Conservative treatment first. Depending on the nerve conduction results, the doctor will decide whether to add physical therapy or, if the test is positive, may consider surgery (outpatient carpal tunnel release) to relieve nerve compression. Results to be discussed at the next visit.
5. Patient agreed with the plan, said she hoped to avoid surgery and try therapy first, and had no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
New consult for breast reduction.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Julia Jones is a 25-year-old female (DOB 5/16/1996) presenting for evaluation of breast reduction. She has not met with anyone about this before. She has considered it for about six or seven years.

She reports pain in the neck and upper back since high school. She has seen a chiropractor for a few years. She is unsure whether all of the pain is from her breasts, but the pain builds up and she thinks it could be attributed to her breasts, especially when working at her desk all day. She said it might be scoliosis but is not sure. She has not had physical therapy and does not take pain medication for it.

She has bra strap indentations in her shoulders. She does not wear a regular bra often and mostly wears a 34E sports bra because it is more comfortable and other bras are expensive in her size. The doctor noted she appeared to be wearing about a G cup. She sometimes has numbness or tingling in the hands and sometimes has nipple pain. She has no rashes under the breasts, but the area is always sweaty. Her activities are limited: she has to hold her breasts during working out, jumping, or running, and it hurts.

She takes propranolol for migraines. Family history: her mother had breast cancer at age 40. She was advised to begin mammograms at age 30 and has not had any. She is otherwise healthy for the most part. She has lost about 10 pounds over the past few months and would like to lose about 20 more. She drinks a little wine on occasion. Tobacco and drug use were asked about, but only alcohol was reported. She is studying psychology. She has no children and may plan to in the future, but is unsure she is interested in breastfeeding.

Insurance: currently Blue Cross Blue Shield, but she will likely switch to her husband's new plan in July, which she believes is not Blue Cross.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Neck and upper back pain since high school. Pain with exercise, jumping, and running. Possible scoliosis per patient, unconfirmed.
Neurologic: Sometimes has numbness or tingling in the hands. History of migraines, on propranolol.
Breast: Sometimes has nipple pain. Bra strap indentations in the shoulders.
Skin: No rashes under the breasts. Breasts are always sweaty.
Constitutional: Lost about 10 pounds over the past few months.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Breast: Inspection shows asymmetrical breasts with severe ptosis bilaterally. One breast is a little lower than the other. There is no nipple retraction or discharge bilaterally. No breast tenderness, masses, or axillary lymphadenopathy is palpable. Measurements were taken.

RESULTS
Minimum required resection, based on a BSA of 2.65 using the Schnur scale, is 1,792 grams, which the doctor stated should be attainable. No imaging or laboratory results were discussed. Mammograms have not been done.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
25-year-old female with symptomatic macromastia presenting for evaluation of breast reduction. The doctor stated that the patient has attempted nonsurgical treatments with minimal relief and is an ideal, or great, candidate for bilateral reduction mammoplasty. Given her extremely large breasts and the measurements, the doctor said there is potential for using a nipple graft.

Plan:
- Photos to be taken today by Catherine. Symptoms are documented in the note for the insurance company.
- Insurance submission for approval of medical necessity will likely wait until the patient is on the new plan in July. The patient will notify the office with the new insurance information.
- After approval, the office will work with her on a surgery date. A pre-operative visit will be held shortly before surgery to review instructions and answer questions.

Surgical counseling by the doctor:
- Anchor-type incision. Tissue is removed and the breast and nipple are lifted to help with back and neck pain and for appearance.
- The patient would like to be a B cup. The doctor said she will probably be a small C and that a B might be a little small, to be determined during surgery. Size is limited by the blood supply to the nipple.
- Surgery takes about 3 hours, with one drain on each side for about 1 week, removed in clinic. Clear plastic tape will be placed over the incisions. Scars may be red at first in lighter skin and take about a year to mature.
- Overnight hospital stay for pain and nausea control.
- About 30% of patients cannot breastfeed after reduction, because both fat and glandular tissue are removed. Breasts will change with weight gain and pregnancy hormones, and may appear somewhat deflated after pregnancy.
- Nipple sensation is usually fine, but there is a slight chance of altered or absent sensation. Bruising is normal.
- Most patients feel relief of back and neck pain almost immediately.
- Activity restrictions: no heavy lifting for about 6 weeks and no driving for 2 to 3 weeks.

The patient had no questions and is ready to proceed once the insurance is switched.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right-sided abdominal pain for several weeks; referred by Dr. Miller after ultrasound showed gallstones.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Bobby is a patient with type 2 diabetes who presents for several weeks of abdominal pain. Dr. Miller obtained an ultrasound that reportedly showed gallstones and advised avoiding high-fat foods. The patient continues to have significant pain and was referred for surgical evaluation.

The pain is located on the right side of the abdomen just below the ribs. He describes it as a squeezing, severe pain that comes and goes. At its worst it is about 8/10. It is accompanied by nausea. It usually begins right after eating, but can also occur a couple of hours after a meal. The patient stated he thinks it could be a stomach ulcer.

He has had low-grade fevers during periods of a couple of days when the pain was really bad. He has felt nauseated but has not vomited.

Diet: His diet was worse before his type 2 diabetes diagnosis. Since then he has cut back on sugar and started a partial keto diet, and has lost about 25 pounds over three months. He reports that the diet has not been hard to follow, his blood sugars are improving, and his diabetes symptoms have improved. He has cut out pork rinds, which were a staple on the keto diet, and says the pain is a little better but persists.

Family history: Both his mother and father had gallbladder disease and had their gallbladders removed.

Activity: Pain has not significantly limited exercise, though he has to be careful around meals. He enjoys nature photography and is looking forward to getting outdoors in spring.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Low-grade fevers during episodes of severe pain. Weight loss of about 25 pounds over three months with diet change.
GI: Right upper abdominal pain related to eating. Nausea. No vomiting.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 128/88, respiratory rate 16, pulse 68, afebrile, SpO2 99% on room air.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No ectopic beats, clicks, rubs, or murmurs.
Lungs: Clear and equal bilaterally to auscultation.
Abdomen: Positive bowel sounds. Soft, nondistended. Slight guarding in the right upper quadrant. No rebound tenderness. Pain with palpation under the right ribs on inspiration; Murphy's sign positive. No peritoneal signs.

RESULTS
Abdominal ultrasound (reviewed by the doctor): Multiple gallstones in the gallbladder. Mild gallbladder wall thickening. Common bile duct within normal limits at 4.1 mm.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Cholelithiasis with mild cholecystitis. In the doctor's assessment, the patient has mild cholecystitis with gallstones. No frank obstruction is appreciated. The gallbladder appears inflamed, likely developing over the last few weeks since symptoms began. There has been no improvement with dietary modification.
- Recommend laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Procedure explained: a few small incisions with a scope and instruments, gallbladder removed through one incision. Expected duration is 1 to 1.5 hours, with an overnight hospital stay for monitoring.
- After surgery, continue to avoid high-fat foods and eat high-fiber foods.
- Recovery: take it easy for the first 24 hours. Walking on solid ground is fine within a day or two. No hiking. Follow-up in about a week, then release to return to outdoor activity.
- Patient had no questions. The nurse will bring in paperwork to be signed. Surgery is planned for next week.

2. Type 2 diabetes. Follow up with his physician (endocrinologist or primary care provider) to make sure diabetes is managed, particularly given the upcoming surgery. Diabetes will continue to be monitored as outlined by those providers.

Cough for 3 days. Follow-up of type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Hannah reports a hacking cough for about 3 days. It began after she was around her sister, who has been sick with similar symptoms. The cough started gradually and she is now coughing up green phlegm. The patient thinks it might be bronchitis but is not sure. Associated symptoms are a little sore throat and some nasal congestion. She denies fever, shortness of breath, body aches, nausea, and vomiting. She has been drinking lots of water and taking over-the-counter cough medication, which does not seem to be working. She was on vacation last week and felt okay during it; she started feeling poorly after getting back. She has seasonal allergies in the spring with some sneezing and runny nose.

Type 2 diabetes: She has been checking her blood sugars regularly, and they run around 120. She was recently started on metformin 500 mg, a new medication for her, and is tolerating it without problems and without diarrhea. She is having a little trouble with sugar intake.

Hypertension: She has noticed her blood pressure running a little high at home, with systolic readings around 140 and diastolic around 70. She takes hydrochlorothiazide every day. She is trying to avoid salty foods.

Family: Everyone is doing well, and she is busy with life.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever. No body aches.
ENT: Sore throat (mild). Nasal congestion. Seasonal spring sneezing and runny nose.
Respiratory: Cough with green phlegm. No shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Overall good per the doctor, except blood pressure elevated at 144/72.
Sinuses: No frontal sinus tenderness. Mild bilateral maxillary sinus tenderness.
Oropharynx: Erythema of the pharynx. Tonsils symmetric with no exudates.
Neck: Anterior cervical adenopathy.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left base, which the doctor noted is still present.
Lungs: Clear, with no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Extremities: No lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Not discussed. A COVID test is to be done today; the result is not available.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Cough, likely upper respiratory infection. The doctor believes it is most likely viral, especially given exposure to someone with similar symptoms.
- Let the virus run its course and treat symptoms.
- Drink lots of fluids and get lots of rest.
- She may try another cough medicine, such as Coricidin HBP, and should be careful with over-the-counter medications because of her blood pressure and diabetes.
- COVID test today, with the patient's agreement. Results will be given to her.

2. Type 2 diabetes. She appears to be doing well.
- Continue metformin 500 mg daily or twice daily.
- Hemoglobin A1c is due at the next visit; it is checked about every 3 months.

3. Hypertension. Blood pressure is elevated in clinic and has been creeping up slightly at home.
- Increase hydrochlorothiazide to 25 mg once daily, taken in the morning because it can increase urination.
- Continue checking blood pressure a few times a week at different times of day.

The patient had no questions.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm.
Abdomen: Soft.
Extremities: No lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
PFTs: Look quite good per the doctor.
Hemoglobin A1c: Indicates blood sugar has probably been running a little high over the past couple of months (value not stated).

1. Diabetes: A1c suggests blood sugar has probably been running high over the past couple of months. The patient plans to return to his diet regimen.
- Increase metformin to 1,000 mg twice a day.
- Repeat hemoglobin A1c in 3 months.
- Continue monitoring blood sugars at home.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
James is a 57-year-old male with a past medical history of congestive heart failure and type 2 diabetes who presents with back pain.

He hurt his back on Saturday morning, about four days ago, while swinging back to hit a golf ball. He felt a pop and immediately had to get down on the ground. He tried to loosen up his back. Congestive heart failure: He reports taking his medications, watching his diet, avoiding salty foods, and trying to exercise regularly. He had a little weight gain over the summer, no more than five pounds. He has no problems lying flat at night. The doctor had not seen him in a while.

Type 2 diabetes: Diet has been a struggle (he loves jelly beans), but he is getting through it. He monitors his blood sugars regularly, though he sometimes forgets. He is still taking metformin.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for back pain and right leg weakness (right foot drop-like symptoms). Denies other symptoms. Denies difficulty lying flat. Weight gain of less than five pounds over the summer; leg swelling was asked about, but the patient did not specifically address it.

Sore throat for 4 days. Follow-up of hypertension and diabetes.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Teresa reports sore throat for about 4 days. She thinks she had a fever last night because she was very sweaty, but she did not take her temperature. She also had chills and sweating last night. Swallowing is very hard and painful every time she swallows. She has trouble eating but can drink; cold water feels good. She drinks mostly water during the day, plus wine at night. She has a mildly stuffy nose, and thinks her tonsils are swollen. She wonders whether this might be mono (patient's own suggestion). No nausea. She has young children in school with runny noses and cough, but no one in the household is complaining of illness. She had strep throat as a child but not as an adult. She works as a cashier in a supermarket. She received the two-dose COVID vaccine series, had a bad reaction (felt sick for about 2 days), and has not had a booster.

Hypertension: She bought a home blood pressure cuff. Readings vary, with systolic sometimes about 120 and sometimes about 140; she does not remember the diastolic numbers. She takes lisinopril 20 mg every morning with a multivitamin and vitamin D. She does not limit salt and likes chips with her wine.

Diabetes: She checks blood sugar only sometimes. Morning fasting readings are about 80-90, and at night sometimes about 140. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily with breakfast and dinner.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Reported fever (felt, not measured), chills, and sweating last night.
ENT: Sore throat, painful swallowing, mild nasal stuffiness, possible swollen tonsils.
GI: No nausea. Difficulty eating due to painful swallowing.
Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Low-grade fever of about 100.4, blood pressure 132/80, heart rate 84.
Face: No pain to palpation of frontal or maxillary sinuses.
Nose: Edema and erythema of nasal turbinates bilaterally with clear discharge.
Throat: Bilateral erythema and edema of the peritonsillar space with exudates bilaterally. Uvula midline.
Neck: Right-sided cervical lymphadenopathy.
Lungs: Coarse rhonchi at the bases that clear with cough.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmur or rub.

RESULTS
Rapid COVID test done on arrival was negative.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Sore throat / upper respiratory infection: The doctor stated the findings are consistent with an upper respiratory infection and expressed concern for possible strep throat.
- Rapid strep swab by the medical assistant.
- If positive, prescribe amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 10 days.
- Lidocaine swish and swallow for pain.
- Ibuprofen as needed for pain and fever.
- Continue to hydrate as much as possible.
- The patient's concern about her children was acknowledged; she had no further questions.

2. Hypertension: Home readings variable.
- Order lipid panel.
- Increase lisinopril from 20 mg to 40 mg once daily to improve blood pressure control, and reassess response.

3. Diabetes:
- Order hemoglobin A1c to determine whether metformin needs adjustment. Continue metformin for now.

She reports a little weakness in the arm, but nothing too significant. She denies fever or chills.

Epilepsy: No recent seizures; her last seizure was about a year ago. She is still taking Keppra.

Depression: She started therapy last year and avoided medication because she is already on Keppra. Therapy has been good and has definitely helped. She still feels a little down and stressed. She denies thoughts of harming herself or others.

Peptic ulcer disease: She had significant stress a year ago with ulcer-related issues, and an endoscopy was done. She is doing better and has had no issues since the procedure.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting.
HEENT: Some nasal congestion from allergies.
Musculoskeletal: Left elbow pain, stiffness, and swelling; mild arm weakness.
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in the hands.
Psychiatric: Feels a little down and stressed. No thoughts of harming self or others.

Vitals: Per the doctor, vital signs in the office look great (values not stated).
Heart and lungs: The doctor planned to auscultate; no findings were stated.
Left elbow: Erythema and edema. Pain to palpation of the left olecranon. Warm to palpation. Pain with flexion and extension, with some stiffness.
Vascular: Palpable left radial pulse.

- Rest.
- Meloxicam 15 mg once daily.
- Ice the area.

- Continue Keppra 500 mg twice daily.
- Refill ordered.

- Start Lexapro 10 mg once daily and monitor response.

4. Peptic ulcer disease: 
- Continue Protonix 40 mg once daily before meals.

Foot pain after a soccer injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jean is a patient who presents with foot pain after an injury during a soccer game yesterday. She was trying to steal the ball from another player, who fell directly onto her foot. Her body twisted around the other player and she felt pain in her foot. She had to stop playing right away and was helped off the field. The transcript is inconsistent about laterality: the patient said the other player fell onto her "right" foot, while the doctor referred to the left foot throughout the visit and the exam and imaging were of the left foot. The doctor's assessment also refers once to "right foot pain." The patient said it might be a bone bruise but was not sure.

She has had many soccer injuries but has never injured this foot before. She has played soccer since age four or five, starting in a local town league and continuing through high school teams.

Since the injury she has been keeping the foot elevated, icing it, and taking ibuprofen. The trainer wrapped it yesterday. Pain is 3/10 with ibuprofen and 7-8/10 without. She denies numbness, tingling, or any strange sensation in the foot.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Neurologic: Denies numbness, tingling, or abnormal sensation in the left foot.
Musculoskeletal: Foot pain as per HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 118/72, heart rate 58, respiratory rate 14, afebrile, O2 saturation 99% on room air.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm. No clicks, rubs, or murmurs. No ectopic beats.
Lungs: Clear and equal bilaterally with good air movement.
Left foot: Bruising on the bottom and top of the foot. Associated swelling. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot. Positive piano key test.
Neurovascular, left foot: Brisk capillary refill in less than 3 seconds. Dorsalis pedis pulse intact and strong. Motor intact. Sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
Diagnostic imaging reviewed by the doctor (obtained before the visit; the type was not stated, and the doctor later referred to it as an x-ray): subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal, 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Foot pain due to a Lisfranc fracture, per the doctor. The doctor described this as a fracture of the second metatarsal at the top of the foot where the metatarsals meet the cuboid. (The doctor's assessment says "right foot," but the exam and imaging were of the left foot.)

Plan:
- MRI ordered to assess for injury to the ligaments at the top of the foot.
- Based on the exam and x-ray, the doctor believes she will most likely need surgery. The surgery would reposition the bones and hold them with plates and screws while they heal, allowing the bones and ligaments to heal properly. It is a day surgery with same-day discharge.
- The doctor recommends surgery because poor bone and ligament healing could lead to loss of the arch and a flat foot, and there is a high likelihood of arthritis in the foot.
- After surgery she will be in a cast and use crutches, with no weight bearing on the left foot for about 6-8 weeks. She will then gradually begin walking on the foot as tolerated, and the doctor will reassess at that point.
- Follow up in clinic.
- She will be out for the rest of the soccer season. The goal is to have her ready for next season.
- The nurse will start her paperwork. The doctor will see her Monday morning for the procedure.
- The patient agreed and thanked the doctor.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after hospitalization for heart failure.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Christina presents for follow-up after a recent hospital admission for heart failure. She reports that before admission her ankles were swelling and would not improve, even when she went to bed. She also had trouble breathing, needed to be propped up in bed to breathe at night, and had difficulty talking. A friend, Diane, advised her to call 911. She was taken by ambulance to the ER. In the transcript the doctor said "i think it could be pneumonia" during this part of the history, but the context is unclear and no pneumonia diagnosis was established.

In the hospital her blood pressure was 200/90. She states she may occasionally miss a dose of her medications but tries to take them all the time. Remembering to take the pills is a "sticky point." She admits to dietary indiscretion, eating salt and vinegar potato chips, which she buys at home, almost every day.

Since the hospital stay she is feeling better. She has less shortness of breath and thinks walking more is helping. She was given a water pill and reports urinary frequency, nearly incontinence. Another blood pressure medication was added, and she thinks she feels a little better on it. She has a home blood pressure cuff but admits she has rarely used it; she plans to use it daily. She denies shortness of breath or sleep problems since returning home and says she is sleeping very well. She denies chest pain.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Felt very unwell before admission; feeling better now.
Cardiovascular: Prior ankle swelling. No chest pain.
Respiratory: Prior shortness of breath and orthopnea. Currently less shortness of breath, none reported since being home.
Genitourinary: Urinary frequency with near incontinence on the water pill.
Neurological/Sleep: Sleeping well.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 128/72, temperature 98.7, heart rate 72, respirations 18, oxygen saturation 96%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously heard and stable.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Lower extremities: Trace edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram (reviewed by doctor): preserved EF of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation.
Blood pressure in hospital: 200/90 (per history).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure: The doctor feels this was caused by dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension.
- Continue Bumex 2 mg once daily.
- Continue to watch diet and avoid salty foods; stop the potato chips.
- Keep a log of blood pressures and food intake.
- Weigh daily and call if she gains 3 pounds in 2 days.
- Referral to a nutritionist for diet education.

2. Hypertension:
- Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily and Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
- Take medications consistently; a pill box or phone alarm was suggested.
- Use the home blood pressure cuff daily.
- Order a renal artery ultrasound to be sure nothing is missed, such as possible renal artery stenosis (doctor's consideration, not a diagnosis).

3. Kidney disease:
- Obtain more labs to make sure she tolerates the new medications.

Follow-up in 3 months. The patient had no questions.

Kidney: he last saw his nephrologist about a month ago. He has been told to avoid NSAIDs and generally does so, but took Motrin for a while about a week ago for foot pain and stopped as soon as he could. He states Tylenol is not very effective for him.

Left ankle pain after an injury.

Matthew is a patient who injured his left ankle yesterday while on a walk with his wife. He stepped off a curb and landed on the ankle wrong. He was able to walk back to the house but it was painful. He reports no substantial prior injuries to the ankle. Since the injury he has taken ibuprofen, elevated and iced the ankle, and kept weight off it. Pain is rated 8/10 without medication and about 7/10 after taking ibuprofen or Tylenol. During the visit the doctor commented early on that it might be a bone bruise but said he was not sure.

Musculoskeletal: Left ankle pain, lateral. No pop heard at time of injury.
No other systems discussed.

Vitals: Stable, a little elevated; the doctor noted the patient is in pain.
Left ankle: Ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus. Swelling and edema present, with soft tissue swelling laterally. Tenderness to palpation on the lateral side. No laxity in the joint. No bony tenderness to palpation of the foot.

Left ankle x-ray, reviewed by the doctor: No fracture or bony abnormalities appreciated.
