CHIEF COMPLAINT
Upper respiratory infection symptoms.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Andrew is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history of depression, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension. He presents with fatigue and shortness of breath that began over the last week or so while doing yard work. He thinks he caught his first cold, since he and others have not been wearing masks as much at the end of summer, and that it got worse. He thinks it could be the flu. He has had both COVID vaccines. He has no history of seasonal allergies.

Shortness of breath occurred mainly with lifting or carrying, such as heavy bags of soil during landscaping, when he became very winded, which surprised him. He is not coughing up anything yet but feels that may be next. He felt a little warm but thought it was from exertion. His elbows hurt quite a bit and his knees felt tired with some tension around them. He attributes the knee symptoms largely to lifting the bags. He denies nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Depression: It has been a "crazy year and a half" and he was a little concerned, but for the most part he has been doing well. His wife got him into barre classes to help him relax, and he thinks they are working. Per the doctor, they previously discussed not starting medication for depression because he takes medication for other conditions.

Type 2 diabetes: He monitors his sugars on workdays but usually forgets on weekends. Diet has been pretty good for the most part, except for some house parties. He reports his sugars have not been elevated since this episode.

Hypertension: He monitors his blood pressure regularly on workdays but not much on weekends. He reports it has been under control. He is taking his medication. He needs a refill of lisinopril.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fatigue. Felt a little warm, which he attributed to exertion.
Respiratory: Shortness of breath with exertion. No cough productive of sputum yet.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Musculoskeletal: Elbow pain. Knee tiredness and tension.
Psychiatric: Depression doing well overall.
Endocrine: No elevated blood sugars since this episode.
Other: Seasonal allergies denied.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Reported by the doctor as normal; no fever.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds strong.
Respiratory: Scattered rhonchi bilaterally that clear with cough.
Extremities: Mild edema of the lower extremities.
Musculoskeletal: Pain to palpation of both elbows.

RESULTS
Chest x-ray: No airspace disease, no pneumonia.
Hemoglobin A1c: 8, mildly elevated. The doctor would like it around 6 to 7 if possible.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Upper respiratory infection: The doctor believes this is a viral syndrome. A COVID test will be sent to make sure he does not have COVID, though the doctor does not think he has it, as he has no exposures. The doctor expects it to resolve in a couple of days. Plan: Robitussin for cough, and ibuprofen or Tylenol for any fever. He should let the doctor know if symptoms worsen.

2. Depression: He appears to be doing well. The doctor offered starting medication or referral to psychotherapy. The patient declined for now and suggested rechecking in a few months.

3. Type 2 diabetes: A1c is 8. Plan: increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily. Repeat hemoglobin A1c ordered, to be done in four months.

4. Hypertension: The doctor feels he is managing it well. Plan: continue lisinopril 20 mg daily, and a refill was ordered. A lipid panel was ordered.

Follow-up: The nurse will help schedule a follow-up appointment in about four months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right knee injury after a skiing fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient was skiing in Vermont last weekend. She caught her ski while coming off the lift and fell. She felt her knee pop, and it has hurt ever since. She was unable to bear weight and had to be taken down the hill by ski patrol. She reports pain on the outside of the knee and a sensation that the knee will not hold her weight and feels like it will buckle. She was able to bend the knee immediately after the injury but not really now. She can straighten it somewhat, but it hurts a lot to straighten fully. She denies numbness or tingling in her toes and thinks she can feel her toes normally. She is taking ibuprofen, which helps somewhat. She declined something stronger. She is using crutches. Early in the visit, the doctor wondered whether this might be a torn meniscus.

Social: She has twin four-year-olds whom she chases. Her husband is home but works a job that takes him away frequently, so she is often alone with the children. She would like to return to running but is currently not very active. Otherwise generally healthy, with no high blood pressure, diabetes, or similar conditions.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain, instability/buckling sensation, decreased range of motion.
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in toes.
Otherwise not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation.
Right knee: Edema and effusion present. Pain to palpation of the lateral knee. Decreased flexion and extension. Positive Lachman sign.
Vascular: Palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. No leg or ankle edema.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right knee: no bony abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right knee injury. The doctor is concerned for a rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), based on the mechanism of injury and the positive Lachman sign. The doctor noted that some people can have a normal exam and still have a torn ACL. Because of the significant lateral knee pain, the doctor also wants to ensure no other structures were damaged.
- Order right knee MRI to confirm the exam findings and evaluate other structures; the doctor hopes to obtain it within the next couple of days, then discuss next steps.
- Continue ibuprofen 600-800 mg every 8 hours as needed for pain.
- Place the knee in a brace for support.
- Continue crutches.
- The doctor asked about activity level to help decide on graft choice if ACL repair is needed.
- The patient had no questions. Follow-up soon after the MRI.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Non-healing wound on the right foot for about 2 to 3 weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Wayne is a patient with diabetes and neuropathy who presents with a wound on the right foot present for about 2 to 3 weeks that is not improving. He was referred by his PCP. He previously saw a podiatrist but that provider moved away, and he was unable to find another. The patient thinks the wound could be athlete's foot. He denies any trauma. He bought a new pair of shoes (Hokas) for travel and, because of neuropathy, did not feel that they were too tight at first. It started as a blister and now looks much worse. He has been putting a Band-Aid on it. He completed a course of antibiotics from his PCP yesterday, and the wound looked about the same. The wound is not painful; he cannot feel it. He denies fever, chills, and drainage. Sometimes his sock sticks to the wound even with a Band-Aid in place. He is no longer wearing the shoes. He likes them because they are comfortable, easy to take on and off, and provide good stability; he reports sometimes having stability issues. He got them at REI a couple of years ago. Regarding his diabetes, he does not think it is too bad; his last HbA1c was a little over 8.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever and chills.
Skin: Non-healing wound on the right foot, no drainage, sock sticks to the wound at times.
Neurological: Neuropathy; cannot feel the wound.
Musculoskeletal: Reports sometimes having issues with stability.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Temperature 98.1, heart rate 72, respirations 16, blood pressure 110/65.
Foot: 1 x 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the right fifth MTP joint. Yellow slough present with minimal granulation tissue. No surrounding erythema or cellulitis. No fluid collection. No necrosis. No odor. No bony exposure appreciated. No tenderness to palpation per patient.
Vascular: Palpable bilateral femoral and popliteal pulses. No palpable DP or PT pulses, but Doppler signals are present.

RESULTS
Right foot x-ray (done before the visit): no evidence of osteomyelitis.
Last HbA1c per patient: a little over 8.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Diabetic foot ulcer, right foot
- Order ankle brachial index (ABI) to assess blood supply and whether the wound can heal.
- Debridement of devitalized tissue in the office.
- Prescribe collagenase ointment once daily to the wound, covered with a dry sterile dressing. Continue until the wound is shrinking and healthy pink tissue is present.
- Surgical shoe to offload pressure.
- The doctor does not think further antibiotics are needed at this time.
- Follow up in 2 weeks.
- May refer to a vascular specialist if the ABI shows blood supply is not optimal for healing.

2. Diabetes
- Glycemic control is important for wound healing. Doctor stated they might obtain a diabetic (nutrition) consult to discuss diet modifications to help lower HbA1c.

The patient had no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
High blood sugar.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Keith is a 58-year-old male evaluated for high blood sugar. He has been checking his blood sugars at home and feels they have been creeping up slightly. Readings have been in the 300s. He said it might be a sinus infection but is not sure. He reports his diet has not changed at all. He does not add sugar to tea, and he thinks most of his sugar intake comes from fruit. He denies fever and chills. He reports a bit of joint pain in the right knee, with no known precipitating event; he only noticed it when the doctor asked. He had nausea a couple of days ago, which he attributes to sitting in the back of a car. He denies burning with urination.

Reflux: he thinks it is a bit better on Protonix and he no longer wakes at night with reflux.
History of congestive heart failure: he has not noticed recent weight gain or fluid retention. He prefers to sleep on his side and could not say whether he has trouble sleeping flat.
Right rotator cuff: previously an issue, now surprisingly good.

Later in the visit, after hearing "Lyme," the patient asked about alpha-gal syndrome, which he fears. He has eaten meat over the last couple of days.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Musculoskeletal: Right knee joint pain. Right rotator cuff symptoms now good.
Gastrointestinal: Nausea a couple of days ago, which the patient attributes to car travel. Reflux improved, with no nocturnal symptoms. Abdominal pain was asked about and not reported.
Genitourinary: No dysuria.
Cardiovascular: No recent weight gain or fluid retention.
Endocrine: Home blood sugars in the 300s.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Thyroid feels a bit enlarged.
Cardiovascular: Heart regular.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Abdomen: Soft.
Musculoskeletal/Skin: Right knee with erythema and an insect bite with associated fluctuance.
Extremities: Lower extremity edema on the right side.

RESULTS
Vital signs: Look good.
Lyme titer: A little elevated.
Rapid strep: Positive.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Hyperglycemia: The doctor's impression is that it is probably related to infections in the body. The elevated Lyme titer can certainly cause elevated blood sugar, per the doctor.
2. Strep, rapid strep positive: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day for 10 days. The patient was told to finish the entire course even if he feels better.
3. Elevated Lyme titer: Order Western blot and PCR for Lyme to determine whether it is acute Lyme disease. The nurse will set up the tests.
4. Alpha-gal syndrome concern: The doctor said he does not think the patient has it, and noted the patient has eaten meat in the last couple of days. The doctor suggested the patient might be having an inflammatory response related to the elevated blood sugar. Tests will be ordered to look into it.
5. Follow-up: The patient should call if anything happens.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right knee injury, with clicking, after stepping off a curb about two and a half weeks ago.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Gregory is a patient who injured his right knee about two and a half weeks ago. He heard a sound while stepping off a curb and turned his ankle outward. He did not fall. The ankle soreness resolved, but the lateral right knee has remained symptomatic. The knee clicks when he walks, but walking is not painful. If he stands on one foot for a prolonged period, such as leaning a foot against a wall, the knee feels locked and he has to ease back into walking. He has no pain at rest. Pain is absent when the leg is elevated or with the foot flat on the floor, but he does have pain when resting the leg on his heel. Clicking is greatest in a full squat, without pain otherwise. He fears this is an injury of some type. The doctor raised the possibility of a meniscus tear early in the visit.

Treatment so far: he has taken ibuprofen at night, which helps him settle and sleep better. It does not affect symptoms during the day, when he works through them. He is not a big pill taker. He ices 20 minutes on and 20 minutes off at least four times daily. This helps in the morning and at the end of the day, but he says it does not change symptoms much. He takes ibuprofen so he does not have swelling overnight.

Course: symptoms have stayed about the same for two weeks. They worsen only with exertion such as gardening or moving pots, and not to the point of staying worse.

Activity: he rides a bike, using a Peloton indoors for the winter, and is not riding currently. He works in sales and is at home.

He has numbness and tingling in the right foot depending on the shoe he wears. This is chronic and not related to this injury. He has broken his right second toe three times over the last ten years.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: right knee clicking, intermittent locking sensation with prolonged single-leg standing, and no pain at rest. Chronic right foot numbness and tingling, not new.
Neurologic: no new numbness or tingling.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Musculoskeletal (right knee): slight edema and a slight effusion. No pain to palpation of the right lateral knee. Full range of motion. Pain only when the knee is pulled outward, via the foot. Positive varus test. Negative Lachman sign.
Cardiovascular: palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibialis pulses.

RESULTS
Right knee x-ray, reviewed by the doctor: no acute fracture or bony abnormality. The doctor said this was not surprising given the mechanism of injury.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right lateral collateral ligament strain, based on the doctor's exam findings. The doctor stated this type of injury can essentially heal on its own and does not think a surgical referral is needed. An initial meniscus tear was mentioned as a possibility by the doctor early in the visit, but the doctor's assessment after the exam was LCL strain.
- Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once daily.
- Refer to physical therapy to strengthen the muscles around the knee, which may help the knee be stronger and prevent future injuries.
- Continue icing.
- If pain persists, the doctor said an MRI may need to be considered.
- The patient had no questions and was told to call if he needs anything.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for hematuria; renal ultrasound performed today.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Kelly Wood is an established patient (DOB 02/15/1979) seen for renal ultrasound because of hematuria. She reports a few episodes of bright red urine, "the color of cherry Kool-Aid," over the past six weeks. Last week, after scheduling this appointment, she passed what looked like two small stones. Last week she also had constant urinary frequency with severe pain on urination. She rated the pain at the time as 8/10. She currently denies flank pain or lower back tenderness and says things have felt a lot better since passing the stones. The doctor wondered whether the urinary symptoms last week might have been a bladder infection.

Medications: Alavert 10 mg daily. Allergies: no known drug allergies.

She acknowledges that she does not drink nearly enough water and drinks more Mountain Dew than anything else. She states a weight of 250 pounds as an example for calculating fluid intake.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Genitourinary: Intermittent gross hematuria over six weeks, with blood nearly subsided per the doctor. Last week, urinary frequency and painful urination. Passed two small stones last week. No current flank pain or low back tenderness.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
The doctor used a default physical exam template, with the following documented updates:
- Abdomen: no flank pain.
- Genitourinary: the dictation states "anti gu"; normal vaginal exam.

RESULTS
Urine dipstick today: negative for leukocytes, nitrates, protein, ketones, bilirubin and glucose. Color yellow and clear. Urobilinogen 0.2, pH 5.5, specific gravity 1.020. Trace amount of intact blood.

Renal ultrasound:
- Right kidney: 10 cm long by 5 cm wide. No stones, masses or hydronephrosis.
- Left kidney: 10.8 cm long by 5 cm wide. 6 mm non-obstructing left renal stone.
- Bladder: 533 mL pre-void, 0 mL post-void.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Hematuria (primary diagnosis). The doctor stated the blood in the urine was due to the kidney stones. She passed two stones last week and the blood has nearly subsided.
2. Chronic urolithiasis (secondary diagnosis). One 6 mm non-obstructing stone remains in the left kidney. Because it is not obstructing or causing pain, the doctor does not recommend surgical intervention at this time.

Stone prevention counseling:
- The doctor noted that kidney stone formation cannot be attributed to one particular cause, but risk is increased by dehydration, family history, certain foods, digestive tract disease and certain medical conditions.
- Drink about half of body weight in ounces of water daily (for example, 125 ounces for 250 pounds). Avoid sugary drinks such as Mountain Dew.
- Avoid foods rich in sodium and oxalate, and animal protein. Limit salty, processed foods, ideally to less than 1,000 mg sodium a day. Reduce beef, poultry, fish and pork.
- Oxalate was explained as an organic acid found in plants that binds to minerals from which stones form. Examples are spinach, chocolate, beets, rhubarb and soy products.
- A written handout on dietary recommendations was given. The patient is motivated and prefers written information.

Follow-up: return next year if no further bleeding or pain. She should call the office sooner for any issues. She should go to the emergency room for severe pain or bright red blood in the urine.

The patient wondered whether this might be bronchitis (patient's own suggestion). The patient reports seasonal allergies ("I think so").

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain after a fall while playing tennis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Brittany is a right-handed patient who presents with right foot pain. About a couple of days ago, while playing doubles tennis, she went to volley the ball, got in front of another player, and fell on top of her foot. She twisted herself around the other player while trying to catch herself and then felt pain in the foot. She thinks it could be a bone bruise. She was unable to continue playing and had to be helped off the field because she could not put weight on the foot. She has injured her other (left) foot previously but not the right.

Since the injury she wrapped the foot with an ace wrap after the game, iced it last night, kept it elevated on a pillow, and took ibuprofen. Ibuprofen helps a little but wears off after a while. She denies numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation and says she can still feel her foot. She plays tennis recreationally with friends and is trying to learn, as she cannot afford lessons.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right foot pain; inability to bear weight at the time of injury.
Neurological: No numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 125/70, respiratory rate 18, temperature 97.1, oxygen saturation 100%, pulse about 60 bpm.
Cardiovascular: No murmur, rub, or gallop; regular rate and rhythm.
Respiratory: A little stridor appreciated; no wheezes or rales.
Abdomen: No rebound or guarding.
Head/skin: Head symmetrical, mucous membranes normal, not hot to touch.
Right foot: Bruising of the plantar and dorsal aspects with associated swelling. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot (the patient responded "no" when asked if palpation hurt, but the doctor documented tenderness). Positive piano key test of the first and second metatarsals. Warm to touch. Neurovascular: capillary refill less than 3 seconds, strong dorsalis pedis pulse, sensation intact to light touch.
Left foot: Normal exam. Capillary refill appropriate, pedal pulses strong, sensation intact.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot (reviewed by the doctor): subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal, 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right foot pain consistent with a Lisfranc fracture, based on exam and x-ray.
- The doctor recommends surgery to place the bones in proper position with plates and screws and to help prevent further complications. Without surgery, the doctor said there can be poor bone alignment or poor ligament healing, which can lead to loss of the foot arch (flat foot) and arthritis in the foot. The doctor highly recommends it.
- MRI ordered to further assess the fracture and any ligament injury.
- The surgery is a day procedure with same-day discharge. The patient will need someone to drive her home, since it is her right foot.
- Postoperative: cast and crutches, no use of the foot for 6 to 8 weeks, then gradual weight bearing based on progress. Follow up in clinic in about 1 week.
- The doctor stated she will be out for the rest of the tennis season, with the aim of setting her up well for next season. Physical therapy recommended after surgery to strengthen the muscles.
- The patient expressed fear of surgery and asked whether it is necessary. She was receptive to the plan ("I suppose so").
- Surgical risks (bleeding, loss of sensation, nerve damage) to be reviewed through paperwork and with the doctor's assistant. The patient was encouraged to ask questions before and after the procedure.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after inferior STEMI with repeat stent placement.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Julia is a patient with coronary artery disease, hypertension, and diabetes, with an RCA stent placed in 2018. She presents for follow-up after an inferior STEMI that required another stent. She reports she had severe, persistent chest pain, went to the emergency room, and was told she needed another stent. She describes the pain as similar to her first heart attack. During the visit the doctor made a brief remark that it "might be acid reflux," stating he was not sure; this was not elaborated on or connected to the plan.

Currently she denies chest pain or shortness of breath. She was seen about six months ago and was doing fine. She walks her dog daily, about 1.5 to 2 miles. Since discharge from the hospital she has noticed mild leg swelling. She always sleeps with a couple of pillows and thinks she may have needed to sit up a little more, but says sleeping is mostly normal. She can afford her medications, has good insurance, and reports taking them as prescribed. She has not adjusted her salt intake; she tried to watch it after her first heart attack but has become less strict, and she acknowledges she needs to resume. She loves pizza (pepperoni, occasionally vegetables) and fries. She reports watching her sugars and takes metformin, wanting to avoid insulin, and walks to stay active.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain. Reports mild leg swelling since hospital discharge. Possibly needing to sit up slightly more at night, but sleep described as mostly normal.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
Otherwise not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Look good per the doctor (no values given).
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Cardiac: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left base.
Lungs: Clear.
Extremities: 1+ pitting lower limb edema.
Right radial artery cath site: Clean, dry, and intact without hematoma. Right radial pulses palpable.

RESULTS
EKG: Normal sinus rhythm, good R wave progression, and evolutionary changes expected after a STEMI.
Echo: Reduced ejection fraction of 35%. Moderate mitral regurgitation was also mentioned in the assessment.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary artery disease, status post inferior STEMI with repeat stent
- Continue aspirin 81 mg daily and Brilinta 90 mg twice daily.
- Continue Lipitor 80 mg daily.
- Continue Toprol 50 mg daily.
- Refer to cardiac rehab for education and to rebuild confidence with regular exercise.

2. Newly reduced left ventricular function (EF 35%) and moderate mitral regurgitation
- The doctor believes the heart muscle may be "stunned" since she reached the cath lab quickly, and expects recovery over time given medication compliance (the doctor's opinion).
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily.
- Repeat echo in about two months.

3. Fluid retention, with the doctor's impression that she is crossing into acute heart failure
- Start Lasix 40 mg once daily.
- Add Aldactone 12.5 mg daily.
- Labs to be obtained.

4. Hypertension
- Blood pressure appears fine. The doctor thinks she will tolerate Aldactone well.
- Nutrition counseling referral to discuss diet options, including reducing or eliminating preserved meats such as pepperoni and finding alternatives.

5. Diabetes
- Managed with metformin; she is monitoring sugars and staying active. The doctor advised that some measures need to be stepped up. No medication changes were discussed.

The patient agreed with the plan. The doctor encouraged her walking and dietary efforts, and will monitor over time.

Right knee pain.

She says it has reached the point where she wants an opinion. Ice and ibuprofen help. Ice and rest make it feel better, and running and activity make it hurt more. The pain is worse toward the end of the day. After she has been on her feet all day, it starts to ache in the afternoon. She reports no family history of arthritis or immune diseases ("I don't think so"). Her primary care provider, Dr. Wood, has discussed the knee with her over the years and referred her to this visit. The doctor wondered early in the visit whether it might be tendonitis.

Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain as above. Left knee feels normal.
Neurologic: No numbness or tingling in the feet.
Not otherwise discussed.

Sophia is a patient who injured her right knee about four days ago while jumping on her child's backyard trampoline, when her leg slipped out from under her. She felt a "little pop" at the time of injury, and the knee swelled up significantly afterward. She has taken ibuprofen and applied ice, which helped a little, but it is still very hard to get around. Standing hurts quite a bit, but she is able to bear weight on the leg. She localizes the pain to the inner part of the kneecap. During the visit, the doctor said it could be a dislocated kneecap.

Diabetes: Her primary care physician's chart shows she is being treated for diabetes. She reports it is going "okay" but that she forgets to check her sugars quite a bit. She describes her diet as pretty good. She takes metformin 500 mg.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain, swelling, and difficulty walking as above.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds normal, no murmurs or gallops.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Musculoskeletal (right knee): Swelling present. Pain on palpation of the medial knee; mild pain, less than medial, on the lateral side. Slightly limited range of motion, with pain on both flexion and extension. McMurray's test negative (checking for meniscus tear).

RESULTS
No test results were available or reviewed. Hemoglobin A1c was not reported.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right knee injury: The doctor is concerned about a torn or injured MCL (medial collateral ligament), based on the pop heard, difficulty with weight bearing, and exam findings. - Straight leg brace.

- Ice the knee once an hour for about 15 minutes.
- MRI of the knee to confirm the suspected diagnosis and evaluate for other damage.
The patient agreed with the plan.

2. Diabetes: The doctor feels she appears to be managing it fairly well, though the patient reports forgetting to check her sugars. Plan:
- Recheck hemoglobin A1c.
- Refill metformin 500 mg; continue taking it.

The patient had no further questions.

Abdominal pain for one week.

Barbara is a 31-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes and asthma who presents with abdominal pain for the past week. The pain is gradually increasing in severity. It is located in both sides of the upper abdomen. It worsens with exercise such as jogging or running, so she has to take it easy. She has had nausea about three times in the past week and has vomited a couple of times. Nausea and vomiting are on and off. She denies fever.

She has been drinking more coffee, starting last week, with intake "pretty bad" toward the end of last week. She has cut back this week to about one cup. She wonders whether the coffee triggered gastritis. At the start of the visit the doctor raised the possibility of a stomach ulcer. Later in the visit she also reported eating a lot of spicy food lately and thinks this could be contributing to gastritis.

Diabetes: She reports it has been under control. She reported a blood sugar value of "eight hundred," which is unclear as transcribed. She takes metformin 500 mg twice daily, increased at the last visit, and thinks it is helping.

Asthma: She has had no recent asthma attacks. She is prescribed Flovent twice daily and albuterol as needed for wheezing. She sometimes forgets Flovent and decreased its use because she has had no attacks. The doctor advised staying on Flovent daily.

The doctor noted a history of moderately heavy alcohol use.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever.
Gastrointestinal: Abdominal pain, intermittent nausea, and vomiting as per HPI. Diarrhea was asked about, and no response was recorded.
Respiratory: No recent asthma attacks.

Lungs: Mild, very faint end-expiratory wheezes. Otherwise normal lung exam with excellent air movement.
Other: Otherwise normal physical exam.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Abdominal pain: The doctor assessed acute gastritis, probably related to caffeine intake. The doctor agreed with the patient that this could be gastritis. Plan:
- Cut back on caffeine.
- Cut back on alcohol, keeping it to fewer than two to three drinks per week.

Bryan is a patient presenting with low back pain. Yesterday he was raking leaves in his yard and felt fine. His partner, who was present and contributed to the visit, reported that the pain is worse when he stands up from bending, and expressed worry because he has a high pain tolerance and would not complain unless it was a problem. The partner also reported that the patient's back did not hurt as much last week when he thought about raking leaves but did not actually rake. The partner stated the pain has been present for about six hours and requested an MRI now. The partner also said the patient had surgery yesterday; this conflicts with the rest of the history, which describes raking leaves yesterday, and was not confirmed by the doctor or patient. The doctor raised the possibility of sciatica early in the visit.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Low back pain, tightening.
Neurological: Pins and needles/tingling in the right foot (right leg).

Back: Some pain with flexion (bending over), no pain with extension (standing back up) per patient report. Pain to palpation around L5.
Neurological/Extremities: Dorsiflexion normal. Pulses equal in all extremities.

RESULTS
X-ray of the low back: normal per the doctor.

- Prescribe physical therapy for stretches and exercises, given the patient's and partner's reports of long-standing inactivity.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chronic back pain for a couple of years, referred by primary care.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Larry is a patient referred by his primary care doctor for back pain that has lasted a couple of years. The patient said it might be arthritis but he is not sure. He reports no fall or accident. The pain began after he moved furniture one weekend. He describes a sharp, stabbing pain in the back that sometimes radiates down the right leg, all the way to the toe, which he feels is the big toe. He also feels he cannot get comfortable, and this is worse when sitting. He reports numbness and tingling, especially in the right leg down to the foot. He denies numbness or loss of sensation in the genital or rectal area, denies weakness, and denies loss of bladder or bowel control.

Prior treatment: he has tried physical therapy. When the pain is very bad, strong pain medications were prescribed, but only temporarily. Surgery was mentioned in the past, and he would like to avoid it. He states that nothing has worked.

He tries to stay active but this has been difficult because of the pain, and he has gained some weight over the past years. He is relatively new to golf and was trying to get into it, and the pain has set him back.

Family history: he cannot recall any family members with spine conditions.
Social history: he quit smoking about twenty years ago.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: back pain radiating to the right leg, as above. Denies weakness.
Neurological: numbness and tingling in the right leg to the foot. Denies genital or rectal sensory loss.
GI/GU: denies loss of bladder or bowel control.
Constitutional: weight gain over the past years.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: reviewed by the doctor, who said they overall look pretty good.
Musculoskeletal back: no overlying erythema or ecchymosis. Midline tenderness at the L4-L5 disk space with right-sided lumbar paravertebral tenderness. Pain with lumbar flexion. Supine straight leg raise test positive.
Neurological: decreased sensation to light touch at the right lateral thigh (L4 dermatome). Patellar and Achilles reflexes symmetrical.

RESULTS
MRI (reviewed by the doctor): disk herniation with nerve impingement.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Chronic lumbar back pain. Based on symptoms, exam, and MRI, the doctor assessed the symptoms as consistent with an L4-L5 herniated disk with radiculopathy. The doctor explained that a disk between the vertebrae is bulging and pinching nerves, which accounts for the leg tingling.

Plan:
- The doctor recommended a corticosteroid spinal injection into the lumbar spine under fluoroscopy to localize the area of pain and reduce the inflammation causing the pain.
- The patient asked whether this would need to be done all the time. The doctor said patients differ and the response will be monitored, with intervals varying by patient, but injections are usually done no more than four times a year.
- The procedure is relatively quick and common, and the patient should be out of the office within an hour.
- The patient agreed. The first injection will be done today if that works for him, otherwise it will be scheduled.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Transition of care follow-up after hospitalization at District Regional Hospital (admitted 06/29/2021, discharged 07/02/2021). Patient also wanted to discuss COVID vaccination.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Michelle King is a 39-year-old female (DOB 05/07/1982) with a history of quadriplegia due to prior spinal cord injury and a suprapubic catheter. Per the doctor's summary of the hospital course, she presented with increasing spasms, lightheadedness, significant constipation, and diaphoresis. In the emergency department she was febrile with a white blood cell count of 23,000. There was concern for ongoing urinary tract infection, and she was treated with IV antibiotics. She also had labile blood pressure, headache, and vomiting. She improved slowly, cultures were obtained and reviewed, and she was discharged after clinical improvement.

At today's visit the patient states she does not think this was a UTI. She believes she was constipated and that the constipation caused her high blood pressure. She hardly had a bowel movement while hospitalized, then had a "massive" bowel movement after getting home and felt much better. She told the hospital staff this on admission. They obtained x-rays but did not think constipation was the cause. She went to the ER because her blood pressure was out of control, causing headache and vomiting, and she had run out of options at home. She asked whether autonomic dysreflexia can affect the white count. The doctor said it typically does not.

The doctor noted that the urine cultures were not very impressive. Her white count has been mildly elevated at times and was normal last year. The doctor said inflammation can raise it, and that she could have been backed up and inflamed. A CT scan was not done, only an x-ray. She feels back to her normal self and is doing well otherwise. She has no pain or discomfort.

Bowel regimen: she takes MiraLAX daily and doubles the dose when she does not go. She had not had a regular bowel movement in a while before admission despite this. She has lactulose, which takes about two days to work and which she describes as a brutal two days. The doctor described lactulose as a rescue medication used with MiraLAX.

The period before admission was extremely hot. She goes out some but tends to stay in more when it is hot.

COVID vaccine: she is unvaccinated. Her concerns are that side effects are unknown, that it is too soon to tell, and that she has heard of "vaccine injury." She feels she is young and healthy enough to beat COVID even though her respiratory function is limited. She takes vitamin C and multivitamins and is closely monitored. She does not get an annual flu shot. She says she is open-minded.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Feels back to normal. Febrile and diaphoretic before and during admission, per hospital course.
Neurologic: Headache and lightheadedness before and during admission, resolved per patient. Spasms before admission.
GI: Constipation and vomiting before and during admission. No current complaints reported.
Pain: Denies pain or discomfort anywhere.
Otherwise doing well per patient.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
The doctor listened to the patient's chest during deep breathing and normal breathing. No findings were stated.

RESULTS
Per the hospital summary: WBC 23,000 in the ED. Urine cultures were reviewed by the doctor and were "not very impressive." An x-ray was done, with no result stated, and no CT scan was done. The doctor noted that WBC was normal last year and has been mildly elevated at times.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute to chronic constipation / recent hospitalization with leukocytosis.
- The patient believes the hospitalization was more likely due to autonomic dysreflexia related to her quadriplegia, triggered by constipation, and less likely a true UTI. The doctor noted she had marked vital sign changes, including blood pressure fluctuations. Early in the visit the doctor wondered whether a pressure sore might be involved, but this was not pursued. The doctor said "maybe that's all it was."
- The doctor thinks heat and mild dehydration may have worsened the constipation. The doctor also said that heat and humidity in late June may have contributed to unusual presentations seen in other patients.
- Her bowel regimen is MiraLAX daily as the primary treatment, with lactulose as rescue for severe constipation.
- Plan: return in 2 to 3 weeks (the doctor also said 3 to 4 weeks in dictation) for updated fasting labs, including a repeat CBC to confirm the white count trends down, and a full cholesterol panel since she is due. The doctor expects it to normalize and does not expect to find another cause, but said that if it stays elevated it would suggest something else going on with her bowels.

2. Quadriplegia, due to prior spinal cord injury. No additional details were discussed.

3. COVID vaccine status: unvaccinated and hesitant.
- The doctor recommends vaccination and considers her high risk because of her quadriplegia. The doctor believes the vaccine is safe, noted that rare side effects such as Guillain-Barré exist, and said the vaccine is the only true preventive measure. The doctor does not believe supplements will necessarily help prevent COVID and is not convinced alternative treatments or monoclonal antibodies would help.
- The patient does not want to get COVID but needs to make her own decision. The doctor describes her as somewhat homeopathic. She will think about it and contact the office with further questions.

Follow-up in 2 to 3 weeks for labs.

Right knee injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Scott is a patient who injured his right knee about three days ago while playing pickup soccer over the weekend. As he went to kick the ball, he felt a pop in his right knee. The patient thinks it could be a meniscus tear.

The knee was swollen, and some of the swelling has gone down. He reports the knee is not moving as well as it used to and seems somewhat limited. Pain is currently 6-7/10, and about 4-5/10 as the swelling has gone down. He has been taking ibuprofen, which helped a little, and he is taking it on a fairly regular basis. He can bend the knee but has pain toward the end of the motion. He can straighten it but feels he has to help get it straight. He can bear weight, but the knee feels very loose and not normal.

He typically sits at a desk for work, and sitting has not been comfortable lately. Per the doctor, he jogs often.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain, swelling (partially improved), limited range of motion, and a sensation of looseness, as described above.
No other systems discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Gait: Marked limp on the right leg when walking.
Right knee: Significant effusion. Slight ecchymosis. Mild tenderness to palpation at the medial joint line. Passive range of motion is difficult, lacking a few degrees of terminal extension (to about 115 degrees) and about 20-30 degrees of terminal flexion, secondary to pain. Positive Lachman exam. Patient reported the knee felt loose and that it hurt at the very end when pulled.
Neurovascular: Bilateral lower extremities intact. Muscle strength 5/5.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right knee injury. The doctor stated that the examination is suggestive of an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. The patient had suggested a possible meniscus tear. The doctor stated the patient may need surgery, but will first review the MRI result and reevaluate.

Plan:
- MRI of the right knee to evaluate the integrity of the ACL. The nurse will take the patient to the scheduler. The doctor will follow up when results are available.
- Meloxicam 15 mg daily to reduce swelling and pain.
- Ice the knee as needed for ongoing swelling and pain.
- Moderate activities. Wear a knee immobilizer and use crutches when walking to limit stress on the knee.
- Work: Limit activities. Because prolonged sitting can be painful and the knee may lock up, do some slight movement of the legs periodically, without stressing them.
- No jogging until MRI results are available and the treatment plan is determined.
- The patient agreed with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
New right eye twitch.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Karen Nelson is a 3-year-old female with no significant past medical history, accompanied by her father, who presents for evaluation of an eye twitch. Her father noticed the twitch a couple of weeks ago and spoke with her pediatrician, who referred her here. The doctor initially remarked that it could be allergies.

Karen reports she sometimes feels her face moving. It does not hurt. She sometimes feels an urge to move her face, and after it moves she feels better. Her father notices the twitch every day for the last several weeks. Frequency varies: some days several times an hour, other days not until late afternoon. The whole side of her face moves for several seconds and then stops, and she appears to blink frequently. Only her face is involved, with no other body parts twitching. She continues whatever she is doing when it happens and does not seem bothered. Otherwise she has been acting normally, eating well, playing with friends, and doing her usual activities. Her father made a video of the twitch to show at the visit.

No history of seizures. No family history of seizures. Her father had never heard of Tourette syndrome, and no one in the family has anything like it. Karen enjoys soccer, where another girl sometimes plays rough with her.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills. Acting normally, eating well.
Neurological: No headache. No seizures. No sleep problems.
Respiratory: No cough.
Other: Not otherwise discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurological: Awake, alert, and oriented x3. Speech clear and fluent. Followed finger with eyes. Gait steady, heel-toe walking normal. Cranial nerves intact without focal neurologic findings. No pronator drift. Sensation intact to touch. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, knees, and ankles.

RESULTS
Not discussed. (The father's video of the twitch was mentioned, but its review was not described.)

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Eye twitch: The doctor believes Karen has a tic. Reasoning given: the same body part moves each time, and Karen reports an urge to blink with some relief afterward. The doctor does not think this is a seizure.
- The doctor explained that tics are common in children, with as many as one in five having a tic during school years. They are brief, sudden, involuntary motor movements. The cause is not fully understood. They typically occur at about 5 to 10 years of age, and most go away on their own within a year (transient tics).
- The tic may wax and wane. It may be more noticeable when Karen is tired, at the end of the day, or when she is stressed.
- Recommend ignoring the tic. Drawing attention to it can make the child self-conscious and may worsen it.
- No treatment at this time, since Karen is doing well and the tic has not affected school or activities. Treatment can be considered if it worsens.
- Father voiced understanding and agreement.

They recur about a couple of times a month, often enough for her to notice. On those days she takes things slowly. The patient thinks the chest pain could be a pulled muscle.

The doctor stated Coumadin 4 mg and Lasix 4 mg a day. She reports no real side effects. Atenolol made her irritable at first, but she has gotten used to it and it bothers her less now.

Cardiovascular: Occasional chest pain, lasting a few minutes, about a couple of times a month.
Respiratory: Occasional shallow breathing with exertion.

She reports past surgery on her left arm and asked whether it matters.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Acne on the face. New visit with her mother.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Kayla Ward, DOB 4/28/07, MRN 384920, is a 7th grade student seen with her mother for acne on the face. It started about two years ago and is present most every day. She has been using Persa-Gel and washing regularly, which she feels helps "a little bit." There is no itching, bleeding, or pain. Chest and back involvement is "not too bad" per the patient.

Current routine: In the morning she wipes her face with water and a washcloth, and occasionally uses an e.l.f. cleanser if she feels greasy. At night she uses the e.l.f. Super Clarity cleanser, then a toner, then Persa-Gel. She considers today a good day for her skin.

Her acne does not flare with periods. She has had regular periods for about two years. Her mother reports the biggest flare was when she started school sports in the fall, with sweating. Her mother notes Kayla has been doing a good job with the facial care regimen, but it does not help as much as they wanted.

Past medical history: none additional. Family history: none additional.
Social history: lives with her parents and sister. Pets include a dog, a bird, and bunnies. She plays basketball, volleyball, and tap. She wears SPF 30 sunscreen in the summer.

The doctor made a comment during the visit that it "could be rosacea."

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Skin: facial acne as above. No itching, bleeding, or pain. Chest and back acne not too bad.
No flare with menses. Regular periods.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Full skin exam performed, except under the underwear and under the bra.
Skin: multiple benign nevi on the trunk and extremities. Scattered skin-colored papules. Open and closed comedones and erythematous papules on the face, primarily on the forehead, with some on the central cheeks and chin. Chest and back relatively spared. The remainder of the exam is normal.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acne, mild to moderate, mostly comedonal with a small inflammatory component (doctor's assessment). The doctor earlier mentioned that it "could be rosacea," but the final assessment was acne. Plan is to start with topical therapy:
- Morning: wash face with a mild cleanser, then apply a noncomedogenic moisturizer with SPF 30 or higher.
- Evening: wash with the same cleanser and let the skin dry. Apply a thin layer of adapalene 0.1% cream to the areas that usually get acne. Start a few nights a week and slowly work up to nightly. If it is very expensive or not covered by insurance, an over-the-counter gel can be tried. Follow with a thin layer of Clean and Clear Persa-Gel to the usual acne areas, then a noncomedogenic moisturizer.
- Counseled that the topical retinoid will cause sun sensitivity, so sunscreen is needed outdoors, and may cause dryness or irritation.
- The patient agreed to the plan.

2. Multiple benign nevi on the arms, legs, back, and abdomen. The doctor stated they all look normal with no worrisome features.

Follow-up in 6 months to assess progress. The family should call the office with questions or concerns before then.

Left shoulder and left elbow pain for about five months following a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jose James, date of birth 9/29/1957, is a new patient. He reports constant pain in the left shoulder and left elbow for about five months, since a fall while going up stairs. The stairs were icy, his feet went out from under him, and he fell on his left side. He states his shoulder and wrist seemed to take the brunt of the fall. The pain is present all the time and is pretty bad at times. The patient said it might be a pinched nerve but is not sure.

The pain is worse with lifting. He has lifted weights two days per week for years and has tried to keep up the routine, but he has been unable to lift more than 15 to 20 pounds. Over the past one to two weeks he has stopped going to the gym because of the pain. He continues to walk about 30 minutes almost daily with his wife, as they have done since he retired from an office job last year.

He has iced the area a bit and has not taken any medication for the pain. Stopping exercise and some icing have helped a bit, but the pain still hurts enough that he came in. He denies numbness or tingling.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left shoulder and left elbow pain as per HPI.
Neurological: Denies numbness or tingling.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Left shoulder and elbow: Tender to palpation at the shoulder and elbow (patient reported pain on pressing both sites). Tender subacromial space. No warmth, erythema, or deformity.
Special tests: Positive Hawkins-Kennedy and Neer's tests. Empty can test normal.
Strength and neurological: Normal proximal and distal upper extremity strength. Median, radial, and ulnar sensation intact. Abduction to 90 degrees intact.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Impingement syndrome of the left shoulder. The doctor thinks the pain is due to this and does not think there is an additional injury or issue with the wrist. The doctor explained that wrist pain may be experienced because of the shoulder, and noted this type of problem is seen after a fall. The doctor agreed that the fall is a likely cause of the symptoms.

Plan:
1. Physical therapy two sessions per week, plus home exercises provided by the therapists. Referral requested for Dr. Martha Rivera. The patient will be called within a day or two to schedule.
2. If physical therapy does not improve the pain, a cortisone injection could be tried. The patient is not opposed to an injection but prefers to try physical therapy first.
3. Continue icing, especially the shoulder, and rest as much as possible.
4. The patient should call or email if symptoms worsen or do not improve with therapy.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hospital follow-up after an anterior STEMI.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Russell Ramirez is a 45-year-old male with past medical history of CAD status post prior RCA stent in 2018, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. He presents for hospital follow-up after an anterior STEMI, now status post drug-eluting stent to the LAD, with newly reduced ejection fraction of 35% and moderate mitral regurgitation.

The patient reports he is doing "alright" and feels pretty well overall. He feels tired every now and then. When he mentioned the tiredness, the doctor commented that it might be anemia but stated he was not sure. He denies chest pain and shortness of breath. He has been taking short walks around the block and staying close to the house, and doing light housekeeping. He hopes to resume walking on new trails near the Rex Center, gardening, and nature photography.

He has always slept with two pillows, which is normal for him, and reports no sleep difficulties. He denies leg swelling and says he has always had thin ankles. He is taking his medications as prescribed since leaving the hospital, has good insurance through his workplace, and the co-pay is manageable. He wants to keep his stent from closing. He was told in the hospital that his heart's pumping is somewhat low and that he might retain fluid in his legs if not careful. He was told to limit salt, and he acknowledges this will be difficult because he likes pizza. The doctor counseled on avoiding salty foods to optimize heart function and allow return to walking and photography.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Intermittent fatigue.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No leg swelling. Sleeps on two pillows, baseline.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Look good per doctor (no values given).
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Cardiac: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base, about the same as last year.
Lungs: Clear.
Extremities: No swelling or edema.
Right radial cath site: Clean, dry, and intact. No hematoma. Palpable right radial pulse.

RESULTS
EKG reviewed by the doctor: normal sinus rhythm, good R wave progression, and evolutionary changes that are anticipated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary artery disease, status post anterior STEMI with drug-eluting stent to the LAD (prior RCA stent in 2018)
- Continue aspirin 81 mg daily.
- Continue Brilinta 90 mg twice daily.
- Continue atorvastatin 80 mg daily.
- Continue Toprol 50 mg daily.
- Refer to cardiac rehab for education and to build confidence for regular exercise. Patient agreed.
- Continue low-salt diet.

2. Newly reduced left ventricular function (EF 35%) and moderate mitral regurgitation
- The doctor thinks the pumping function will improve in time. He believes the heart muscle is stunned because the patient reached the lab quickly, and notes the patient is adherent to medications.
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily.
- The doctor does not think a diuretic is needed at this time.
- Add Aldactone 12.5 mg daily.
- Labs next week.
- Repeat echocardiogram in about two months.

3. Hypertension
- The patient's blood pressure seems fine at this time.
- Patient to check blood pressure periodically.
- Continue to monitor. The doctor expects the patient to tolerate Aldactone well.

The patient wonders whether it might be a rotator cuff tear.

Pain is located at the back of the right shoulder. Raising the shoulder toward the ear is painful. He has had no numbness or tingling in the fingers. Grip is intact and he can hold a cup of coffee, but he avoids lifting heavy items. Picking up a box from the driveway was difficult. He has taken Tylenol, which kept the pain at the same level but did not reduce it. Symptoms are unchanged since the injury. He denies neck injury or neck problems, and denies pain in the elbow, wrist, or other joints. No prior injury to this shoulder.

He reports a slight headache and says he hit his head a little bit during the injury. He did not lose consciousness. No fever.

Past surgical history: appendectomy for appendicitis about 3-4 years ago. No other medical problems reported.

The patient does not know what caused the ulcer. He has been working in the backyard and is always outside. He thinks he could have stepped on a nail or injured it during other work, but he is unsure whether this caused it.

Diabetes: Blood sugars have mostly been running a little higher than normal. His last hemoglobin A1c was definitely above 9, per the patient.

Claudication: He denies calf pain with walking, saying he just knows it is there. He has not been going on long walks and has been taking it easy lately, mostly staying around the house.

Coronary artery disease: He had a heart attack in 2018 and had a stent placed in the right coronary artery. He takes baby aspirin daily. He denies chest pain or shortness of breath.

He does not have a podiatrist for yearly foot exams.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever or chills.
Neurologic: Frequent tension-type headaches in the front of the head; the patient is unsure whether stress is the cause. Occasional numbness and tingling in the feet, especially in the cold.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No calf pain with walking.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath.
Musculoskeletal/Skin: Right foot ulcer without pain.
Endocrine: Blood sugars running somewhat high.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Afebrile. Blood pressure 127/80. Heart rate in the 60s.
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base.
Lower extremities: No palpable dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pulses. There is a 2 x 3 cm ulcerated lesion on the right lateral foot near the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint. 3. Coronary artery disease, status post right coronary artery stent in 2018. Continue statin. The doctor will talk to the cardiologist about medical clearance in case a procedure is needed.

Nonhealing right foot ulcer.

He saw his PCP before this visit, and the PCP started a medication. He has not yet picked it up from the pharmacy and does not recall the name, but says he has taken it before. The PCP did not give him a surgical shoe but mentioned that this office might provide one.

Musculoskeletal/Neurologic: Occasional throbbing in the foot, no specific pain.
Other systems not discussed.

Right foot: 1 x 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the fifth MTP joint. Redness, drainage, and surrounding edema present, with fluid coming from the wound. No necrosis, no odor, and no bony exposure appreciated. On palpation the patient reports no pain, only a sense of increased pressure that is not distinct. The doctor thinks there is an infection.

RESULTS

- Follow up with PCP for a treatment plan if one is not already in place.

Ongoing management of rheumatoid arthritis; persistent right knee swelling and pain.

The patient reports it helped for maybe a couple of weeks. The knee has remained swollen and painful, and the swelling has now spread to the whole leg. Swelling of the knee has been present for about two months. Pain is about 3/10 now and typically about 6/10 on a normal day. He has worn compression socks much of the time, which help to some degree, but swelling persists, especially around the knee. He has slowed down somewhat. Pain is worst after sitting for a while, when getting up; he is very stiff and uses a cane to get his bearings. The stiffness loosens after a short time. He reports taking Xeljanz XR daily (he thought 11 mg daily) and Celebrex 200 mg daily, started about 2 months ago. Celebrex worked pretty well until the swelling returned. The doctor stated it might be gout but was not sure. The patient reports he loves salty snacks. He has not discussed the leg swelling with his primary care doctor. Physical therapy was previously arranged some years ago for the other knee.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain, swelling, and stiffness on rising after sitting; leg swelling. Pain on fully straightening the knee.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

RESULTS
CMP levels were stated by the doctor to be good this time. Procedure (right knee aspiration and injection): 3 mL of initially clear fluid, then blood-tinged fluid, was aspirated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

- Physical therapy referral.
- If nothing helps, the doctor said a surgery consult might be needed.
- Continue Xeljanz XR and Celebrex 200 mg daily.
2. Leg edema.
- X-ray to look for cause.
- Continue compression socks, reduce salt intake, and elevate feet whenever possible, especially at night.
- If no improvement, make an appointment with PCP. Patient will follow up with PCP.
3. Medication monitoring (Xeljanz, described by the doctor as high-risk).
- CMP every couple of months. Levels good this time. Patient to schedule blood work before next visit.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right elbow pain, medial side.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Teresa presents with pain on the inside of her right elbow that has lasted about four days. The pain radiates down the medial aspect of her arm. She does not recall hitting the elbow on anything and has no prior elbow injury. She rates the pain as 7/10. It wakes her at night when she rolls over. Ibuprofen has not helped. She tried ice briefly at the start. The pain is not improving, though she does not describe it as worsening. She has been doing a lot of pottery on a wheel, working on a ceramic bowl for her son's birthday, and cannot work on it now because of the pain. Early in the visit the doctor raised the possibility of a pinched nerve but said he was not sure.

Hypertension: She is on lisinopril 10 mg and sets an alarm to take it. Home blood pressures have been about 110s to 130s (she said "one teens to one thirties").

Diabetes: She is on metformin 500 mg twice daily. She sometimes forgets doses because she is out and about. Home sugars are sometimes higher, about 150 to 170. She has a sweet tooth and bakes often (cakes, cinnamon rolls) and tastes what she bakes. She had a diabetic consult a long time ago and is interested in seeing a dietitian again.

Exercise: She walks in the morning and evening, about 1 to 2 miles daily.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right medial elbow pain with radiation down the medial arm, as above.
Sleep: Pain wakes her at night.
Other systems were not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 120/70. Respiratory rate 18. Temperature 97.9. Oxygen saturation 100%. Pulse described as appropriate (no value stated). Pain 7/10. Weight is about 5 lb higher than at the last visit.
Cardiovascular: No murmur, rub, or gallop. Pulses equal bilaterally.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Right elbow: Moderate tenderness at the medial epicondyle. No rash, bruising, swelling, discoloration, or lesions. Pain with resisted pronation of the right forearm. Pain with wrist flexion. No pain with supination (turning the wrist outward, as with opening a doorknob).

RESULTS
Right elbow x-ray: Per the doctor, no fracture or bony abnormality. This supports a tendon-related problem.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right elbow pain, consistent with medial epicondylitis (overuse and damage to the tendons), per the doctor.
- Rest the arm. A sling for the right arm will be ordered, to be worn while awake.
- Ice for 20 minutes three times a day.
- Ibuprofen 600 mg (three pills) every six hours with food for one week.
- Hold pottery for the next couple of weeks to allow healing.
- Physical rehab may be considered if healing takes longer. To be discussed at the next visit.

2. Diabetes, long-standing.
- Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily.
- Check and record blood sugars daily.
- Order A1c.
- Refer to diabetic counseling/dietitian.
- Follow up in a couple of weeks. Other medication options may be evaluated if sugars cannot be better controlled.
- The doctor advised cutting down on tasting her baking.

3. Hypertension.
- BP is improved at 120/70. The doctor said this suggests the medication is working and that the walking is probably contributing.
- Continue lisinopril 10 mg.

4. Weight: The 5 lb increase is within normal fluctuation. The doctor was not seriously worried. He suggested it might be muscle, given her walking. Further discussion would follow if she gains another 5 lb.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Emergency room follow-up for chest pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Roger is a 62-year-old male who presents for follow-up after an emergency room visit for chest discomfort. Over the weekend he was doing yard work in very hot weather and developed shortness of breath and mild chest pain lasting about an hour. He became nervous and went to the ER. The doctor wondered whether this might be heat exhaustion. He has never had this before. He reports feeling fine since the yard work was finished and has had no other symptoms since. He has no family history of heart disease in his immediate family, but there is heart disease on his cousin's side of the family. He had knee surgery a couple of months ago and reports no problems with rehab and recovery. He had no chest pain during physical therapy exercises. He has a history of high blood pressure. In the ER, staff were a little concerned about his blood pressure, which was about 180/95 on arrival per the doctor's review of the record. After a few hours of observation it seemed to regulate, and it did not seem to be a problem when he went home. He states his blood pressure usually does not run that high. Current medication includes lisinopril 10 mg daily.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Shortness of breath during the yard work episode; none reported since.
Cardiovascular: Chest pain for about an hour during the episode; no chest pain with PT exercises; no other symptoms since.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Slightly enlarged thyroid, non-tender. Right carotid bruit.
Lungs: Clear.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. 3/6 systolic ejection murmur.
Abdomen: Soft.
Musculoskeletal/Extremities: Healed scar on the right knee from prior surgery. No lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Blood pressure: Still high at this visit (value not stated). ER blood pressure was about 180/95.
EKG: Normal.
Echocardiogram: Somewhat low pumping function of the heart, per the doctor.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Episode of chest pain. The doctor's impression is that it could be related to severe hypertension or could be related to heart disease. Echocardiogram shows somewhat reduced pumping function, which the doctor said will need to be looked into.

Plan:
1. Start carvedilol 25 mg twice a day, which the doctor said helps with coronary disease as well as heart pumping function.
2. Order cardiac catheterization to check for blockages in the heart arteries that could be responsible for the chest pain. The nurse will come in and the cath will be scheduled.
3. Hypertension: Add carvedilol and continue lisinopril 10 mg daily. The doctor will monitor how blood pressure does on this regimen.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Abdominal pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Karen is a 34-year-old female with a history of chronic migraines and hypertension who presents with abdominal pain. The pain began about 10 days ago as mild discomfort on the right side and has worsened over the last couple of days. Severity waxes and wanes, generally 4-5 out of 10, sometimes reaching 7-8 out of 10. It is usually a little worse after meals and not too bad in the morning before eating. It is pretty localized to the right side and low, and may radiate a little to the left. She reports nausea and a little heartburn but no vomiting. The area is a little tender to pressure, and certain positions make it a little worse at its peak. She reports no urinary symptoms, no change in bowel habits, and no blood in stool. Appetite is decreased because of nausea, and she has felt a little more fatigued over the past week. She has had chills but no documented fevers. She has not eaten anything unusual, has had no recent travel other than within Wisconsin, and has had no other exposures. During the visit the doctor briefly said it might be a stomach ulcer but stated he was not sure.

Migraines: Rare recently. They usually respond to Excedrin Migraine. She uses sumatriptan when the over-the-counter analgesic does not work. No recent migraine.

Hypertension: She checks blood pressure about 2-3 times a week, not daily. Readings are usually in the 120s to low 130s systolic and 70s diastolic. She takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and is running low, needing a refill. She also requests a sumatriptan refill.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fatigue over the last week and chills. No documented fevers. Decreased appetite.
GI: Nausea, mild heartburn, right-sided abdominal pain. No vomiting, no change in bowels, no blood in stool.
GU: No pain with urination, no blood in urine, no urinary symptoms.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior exam. Otherwise normal cardiovascular exam. The doctor noted blood pressure appeared a little elevated today.
Abdomen: Mild to moderate right upper quadrant tenderness. Equivocal Murphy's sign in the right upper quadrant (pain with deep breath and palpation). The rest of the abdomen is soft without significant tenderness. No right lower quadrant tenderness with deep palpation.
Back: No CVA tenderness.
Constitutional: No fever today.
Remainder of the exam is normal and unremarkable.

RESULTS
No results available. Tests were ordered today (see plan).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute abdominal pain with right upper quadrant tenderness. The doctor is concerned this may be a sign of gallstones or possibly a gallbladder infection. Plan: CBC, chem 12, urinalysis, pregnancy test, and right upper quadrant ultrasound, to be done right away in the office. The patient will remain in the clinic and should not eat anything for now in case something requiring surgery is found (considered unlikely but possible). She will be sent to the emergency department if results warrant. The doctor will follow up on results before she leaves and hopes she can go home today.

2. Chronic migraines. Occasional episodes, none recent. Continue Excedrin as needed and sumatriptan as needed for breakthrough pain. Continue to avoid alcohol and caffeine binges and get enough sleep. Sumatriptan refill to be prescribed.

3. Hypertension. Blood pressure appears adequately controlled per the doctor. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily with refill sent to the pharmacy. Continue checking blood pressures daily.

Follow-up in about 4 weeks.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain and stiffness after a motor vehicle accident; here for a second opinion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez is a 50-year-old right-handed male (DOB 1/12/71) who works as an x-ray technologist. He is here for a second opinion about his right index finger. In March of this year (about three months ago) he was a passenger in a car that was rear-ended and hit multiple times. He felt two bumps that slung him forward and caused him to stretch out his right index finger. He felt as if he had laid on the finger and that it went backward. The record describes a hyperextension injury. The patient said it might be a dislocated finger but was not sure.

He has had pain since the accident. He cannot make a fist, the pain is sometimes unbearable, and even driving hurts. The finger is still swollen.

He was seen at Point May Orthopedics, largely by the physical therapy staff and a PA. He was referred to occupational therapy and has done therapy. The records state he was scheduled to see Dr. Alice Davis, but it does not appear that he did. An MRI was obtained because of concern for capsular strain with or without rupture of the FDS tendon. The patient understood that the MRI showed a tear, and that the orthopedist would not do an injection because it might worsen the tear. He also reports being told that the orthopedist did not want to do surgery but would do an injection. He is confused by the conflicting messages. Occupational therapy told him the tear is the reason for the restrictions, and he was told not to keep rubbing the finger or using the hand. He tried a splint he bought himself, thinking it would straighten the finger. Occupational therapy tried maneuvers to straighten the finger, but it hurt afterward and the whole finger swelled up. He feels he is not getting medical care.

He was previously offered an injection but did not want a steroid because of a reaction to dexamethasone, which makes his heart race. The doctor noted itching with methylprednisolone, which the patient confirmed, saying it itched "like crazy."

No diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis. He takes a blood pressure pill and no other chronic medications. He has no therapy currently scheduled.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Right index finger pain, swelling, and inability to make a fist. Pain with driving.
Neurologic: Finger felt "a little numb" during the exam.
Cardiovascular: Heart racing with dexamethasone (reported reaction).
Skin: Itching with methylprednisolone.
Endocrine: No diabetes.
Rheumatologic: No rheumatoid arthritis.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Very pleasant, cooperative, healthy male in no distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. 2+ radial pulse.
Right hand: No swelling or bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases, slightly diminished over the PIP of the index finger compared with the middle finger. The index finger rests in about 10 degrees of PIP flexion. Pain when the doctor pushed on the finger while correcting this, and less pain at another spot, with a feeling of numbness. Pain with active flexion of the fingertip ("feels like it's tearing in there") and with passive bending at the MCP joint. The doctor judged the pain to be from stretching because the patient has not been moving the finger for so long.

RESULTS
MRI of the right index finger, 4/24/2021 (obtained at Point May Orthopedics, reviewed by the doctor): focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint, partial-thickness tear of the right FDS, and fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. The radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint and the MCP joint capsule were intact. The extensor tendons were also deemed intact.

X-rays, four views of the right hand, today: no bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout all lesser digits, no concerning soft tissue shadows, and no arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Post-traumatic, rather severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger. The doctor explained that the MRI shows a partial tear of one half of the FDS tendon, the less important of the two flexor tendons, and that the FDP, which goes to the fingertip, is fine. In the doctor's opinion, scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS tendon are blocking excursion of the other tendons so they cannot get through to the pulley. The finger is stiff and sore, and the collateral ligaments and extensor tendons are intact. The doctor said moving it will not tear anything or break a bone.

Plan:
1. Steroid injection into the flexor tendon sheath (trigger finger injection) of 1 cc betamethasone (Celestone) with 0.5 cc lidocaine, avoiding dexamethasone because of the reported reaction. The doctor described it as fairly low toxicity with high benefit, expected to decrease pain and encourage movement. Expected benefit begins in about 3 to 5 days, with further improvement over the next couple of weeks. It will not eliminate the pain but should make it tolerable so he can make gains. The injection may need to be repeated. The patient agreed.
2. Procedure note: The first attempt was stopped because the patient had a dramatic, violent painful reaction to needle introduction, with contortions of the hand and withdrawal of the hand, raising concern for a secondary needle stick. The needle was withdrawn. The patient was counseled on the importance of getting therapeutic steroid into the flexor tendon sheath. A second attempt was made with the same technique and doses (1 cc Celestone, 0.5 cc lidocaine). A small palmar vein bled a scant amount, which was cleaned up and a Band-Aid applied. The patient was reassured repeatedly that no harm was done to the finger.
3. Ice the finger this evening and take ibuprofen.
4. Start moving the finger. A splint immobilizes rather than helps motion. The goal is full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions.
5. Outpatient therapy prescription: once a week for six weeks, preferably with the same therapists as before, for accountability.
6. Driving is safe. The finger may feel odd.

1. Post-traumatic, rather severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger.

The doctor believes scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS tendon are blocking excursion of the other tendons so they cannot get through to the pulley. Collateral ligaments and extensors are intact, so the finger is stiff and sore and the doctor said he will not tear anything or break a bone by moving it.

The doctor described it as fairly low toxicity with high benefit, intended to reduce pain and encourage motion. The patient had a dramatic, violent painful reaction to needle introduction, with contortions and withdrawal of the hand, raising concern for secondary needle stick. The needle was withdrawn. He was counseled on the importance of getting therapeutic steroid into the flexor tendon sheath, and a second attempt was made with the same technique and doses. A small palmar vein bled a scant amount, which was cleaned and a Band-Aid applied. He was reassured several times that no harm was done to the finger.
- Aftercare: ice this evening and ibuprofen.
- The patient was told it is safe to drive, though it may feel a little weird.
- Splint immobilizes and does not help motion. Patient must actively bend the finger, including the MCP, as hard as he can.
- Therapy: outpatient prescription for once weekly for six weeks, preferably with the same prior therapists, for accountability. The goal is full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions. He has no therapy currently scheduled.
