CHIEF COMPLAINT
Bilateral hand numbness and tingling.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ms. Taylor is a 60-year-old right-handed female (DOB 5/4/1961, MRN 0000123), a new patient referred by Dr. Jacob Ward for evaluation of bilateral hand numbness and tingling. The doctor personally reviewed the CT brain with and without contrast done 2/5/21.

The patient reports numbness and tingling for a few weeks in both hands. She noticed it more after her bilateral wrist fractures from a car accident last December, once they had healed. She thinks it could be a pinched nerve. Both hands have worsened over the last month. She wears a splint on the right wrist and sometimes on the left; the right is worse. The splint seems to help. She states her wrist was in worse shape when she broke it than it is today.

On the right, symptoms are most noticeable from the middle and ring fingers up to the forearm. On the left, symptoms are more in the pinky and ring fingers, not the middle finger. She describes the hands as mainly sore, sometimes throbbing, and feeling weaker, especially with use. Tingling occurs more often; when pain occurs it goes away and the tingling is then dull. Symptoms are worse at night and come and go during the day. She denies definite loss of sensation, though the hands may be less sensitive than they should be, and she can still feel. She was given nerve pain medication but has not been taking it as prescribed.

She also reports mild neck stiffness. She hit her head in the accident and was told it was a contusion.

Medical history: chronic kidney disease, gout, hypertension, anxiety, GERD, and diabetes. The patient states she had pre-diabetes that she controlled through diet. No history of thyroid issues.
Medications: carvedilol 25 mg twice daily for hypertension; Lexapro 10 mg daily for anxiety; nerve pain medication (not taken as directed).
Allergies: sulfa drugs (rash).

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fatigue and weight gain.
Eyes: Floaters.
Cardiovascular: Shortness of breath and leg swelling.
GI: Excessive appetite and bloating.
Endocrine: Positive for diabetes; always hungry.
Skin: Nail bed trenches, dryness, itching.
Musculoskeletal: Gout, muscle pain. Mild neck stiffness (per HPI).
Neurological: Paresthesia in both hands.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurological: Sensation normal except pin prick sensation diminished in the third and fourth fingers on the right and the fourth and fifth fingers on the left. Reflexes 1+ and symmetric, 2+ at the knees. Toes down-going bilaterally. Tinel's sign positive at both wrists and both elbows.

RESULTS
CT brain with and without contrast (2/5/21), personally reviewed by the doctor: no metastatic disease, no acute intracranial abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome.
2. Question of bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome.

The doctor discussed the impression with the patient. Plan: schedule EMG/NCV. If symptoms do not resolve, consider hand clinic referral for possible symptomatic injections or carpal tunnel release surgery, which she may also pursue through her current orthopedist. The patient is encouraged to wear her splints. Return for EMG/NCV. The doctor also planned to look up the nerve pain medication the patient mentioned.

Six-week postoperative follow-up after right medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty. Patient reports persistent numbness on the side of the knee.

Stephanie Morales (MRN 113322) is a 44-year-old female who presents six weeks status post right medial unicompartmental arthroplasty. She reports the knee is doing well and says she has no problems and no pain. She is very happy with how the surgery went. She still has numbness on one side of the knee. The doctor said it might be a pinched nerve but that he was not sure. He also said the area of numbness should get smaller as the nerves that supply the skin across the knee heal. She is doing physical therapy.

She works for UPS and has not been able to return because her position requires going up and down steps. Her employer has asked her to return to a position where she can sit for the shift with breaks. She asked for a note excusing her from work for another six weeks. She also asked about driving.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: No knee pain. Persistent numbness on the side of the right knee.
Other systems: Not discussed.

Gait: Antalgic with a slight limp and decreased velocity. No assistive device used.
Right knee: Healed surgical scar. Mild swelling. Tenderness over the area of the incision. Range of motion 0 to 120 degrees. The remainder of the exam was normal. The doctor noted the incision looks good.

RESULTS
Three-view radiographs of the right knee taken today show implants in stable position and well aligned. There is no evidence of loosening or early complications. No intervention was done under the kneecap.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Six weeks status post right medial unicompartmental arthroplasty, recovering well.
- Continue physical therapy for strength, range of motion, and endurance.
- The doctor expects further improvement. He noted she may still have occasional aches and pains and that people usually feel back to themselves in two to three months.
- Follow up in six weeks by telemedicine visit to check progress. The front desk will schedule it.

2. Numbness on the side of the knee.
- The doctor said it might be a pinched nerve but was not sure. He expects the numb area to shrink as the cutaneous nerves heal.

- Restrictions: no lifting over 5 to 10 pounds, and no standing or sitting longer than 30 minutes. The doctor said this usually means she cannot do a UPS job.
- A note excusing her from work for another six weeks will be provided by nurse Anna.

4. Driving.
- The doctor said data show normal reflex time returns by six weeks. Return to driving depends on when she feels ready and safe.

Left knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Angela is a patient who presents with left knee pain that began about one week ago. She was running around with her niece, who is learning to ride a bike without training wheels, when she fell and thinks she twisted her knee in an awkward way. She heard a pop when it twisted. She has been limping since the injury and reports it has not improved. Pain is felt on both sides of the knee, more on the medial side than the lateral side. Pain started at about 4/10 and she feels it is getting worse. She describes it as throbbing.

She has a recent history of an ulcer, and her doctor told her not to take NSAIDs such as Advil or ibuprofen. She has been taking Tylenol, which helps a little, but the pain returns within one to two hours, and she is not supposed to take it more often than about every four hours. She has also wrapped the knee with kinesiology tape.

Early in the visit, the doctor wondered whether this might be a meniscus tear.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left knee pain and limping as per HPI.
No other review of systems was discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Left knee: Edema present. Effusion present. Moderate range of motion, able to move the knee but not through full range. Pain with flexion and extension. Tenderness with palpation of the medial side of the knee. Lachman's test negative. Valgus and varus stress tests negative.

RESULTS
Left knee x-ray: Normal. No fractures or bony abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Left knee pain, assessed by the doctor as a likely MCL (medial collateral ligament) strain, from a twisting mechanism during the fall. Based on the exam, the doctor does not think anything is torn. The strain does not seem too bad.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Evaluation of kidney stones (referred by PCP).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mason is a patient referred by his PCP for evaluation of a kidney stone. About one week ago, while moving hay in the barn with horses, he developed sudden-onset right back pain. He initially thought it was from throwing hay, but he broke out in a sweat and became very nauseated. He saw his PCP, who ordered a CT scan and told him he had a kidney stone. He has never had a kidney stone before. His father has had kidney stones many times.

The pain radiated almost down to the groin, but not all the way. Since the initial episode, the pain has recurred a couple of times but did not last as long. He has been straining his urine as instructed and has not seen anything in the strainer. He has not noticed blood in his urine, and it has not been darker than usual.

During the visit, the doctor wondered aloud whether the initial pain might be a pinched nerve.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Sweating at onset of pain. No fever noted on vitals.
GI: Nausea at onset of pain.
GU: No hematuria. Urine not darker than usual. Right flank/back pain radiating toward the groin as above.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: No fever; blood pressure and heart rate normal per the doctor.
Abdomen: No tenderness to palpation. No rebound or guarding.
Back: Right CVA tenderness. The doctor explained this is expected with a kidney stone.

RESULTS
CT (reviewed by the doctor): 0.5 cm stone in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right proximal ureteral kidney stone, 0.5 cm, without hydronephrosis.
- Push fluids to facilitate passing the stone.
- Prescribe oxycodone 5 mg every 6 to 8 hours for pain. May use Tylenol between doses for breakthrough pain.
- Continue straining urine until the stone passes.
- Order BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture. Based on the urinalysis, will determine whether antibiotics are needed for possible infection.
- Follow up in about 1 to 2 weeks. If the stone has not passed by then, will discuss further treatment, including lithotripsy (shock wave to break up the stone, described by the doctor as not very invasive).
- Nurse to bring in the prescription.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chronic abdominal pain with constipation and diarrhea (new patient referral to GI).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patrick Allen is a 42-year-old man (DOB 7/7/1977) with a past medical history of GERD, anxiety, and depression, referred for abdominal pain and diarrhea.

He reports on-and-off pain in the mid abdomen, just below the umbilicus, for about two years. He describes it as a nagging feeling that bothers him at times and not at others. He went to the ER a few months ago, where an abdominal CT was done. He was told nothing was seen on the scan. The patient wondered whether this might be lactose intolerance.

Over the past couple of months he has had alternating constipation and "explosive" diarrhea. Before that, his bowel movements were normal. He has more constipation than diarrhea. When constipated, he usually does not go, and the stool is hard when he does. He has bowel movements about 3-4 times a week when constipated. He reports that massaging the abdomen makes it feel like stool is moving, and he can eventually go. Pain improves a little after a bowel movement. Diarrhea depends on what he eats; he has a sensitive stomach and expects diarrhea after pasta with a creamy sauce. It is usually a single episode and then resolves, not lasting multiple days. No blood in the stool.

He denies nausea, vomiting, heartburn, or indigestion, and is eating and drinking okay. Weight is stable, though he says he could stand to lose about 25 pounds.

Family history: his sister has irritable bowel syndrome, which is what he has always thought he had, though he has never been diagnosed. No family history of GI cancer or liver disease. No abdominal surgeries; gallbladder and appendix are intact. No prior colonoscopy.

Labs: he had a physical about four months ago with blood work. His PCP told him he had very slightly elevated ALT and AST, to be rechecked in about six months.

Medications: Crestor (about 18 months) and olmesartan daily; Tylenol hardly ever, about once a month. Alcohol: a couple of beers after yard work on Saturdays. No history of heavy alcohol or drug use.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Weight stable.
GI: Positive for abdominal pain, constipation, and intermittent diarrhea. Negative for blood in stool, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, and indigestion.
Hematologic: No excessive bruising or bleeding.
Extremities: No ankle or foot swelling.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants. Mild tenderness on palpation of the left side near the umbilicus. Stool palpable in the lower colon, consistent with increased stool burden. Slight hepatomegaly in the right upper quadrant.
Eyes/Skin: No jaundice.
Lungs: Clear.
Cardiovascular: Normal heart sounds bilaterally, no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
The remainder of the exam was normal per the doctor.

RESULTS
Abdominal CT 1/23/2020: normal CT of the abdomen. The doctor agreed it looked normal.
Recent labs (patient report, about four months ago): ALT and AST slightly elevated per his PCP. No values available.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Chronic abdominal pain with constipation and intermittent diarrhea. The doctor thinks this is constipation with occasional diarrhea related to certain foods. The doctor noted that colonoscopy can be considered for unexplained abdominal pain and bowel habit changes, but none was ordered.
- Start a fiber supplement now.
- Increase water intake to at least 48 ounces daily.
- Be mindful of foods that trigger diarrhea and avoid them.

2. Slight hepatomegaly with previously reported mildly elevated liver enzymes. The doctor did not think the liver finding explains the abdominal pain or bowel changes. The doctor listed possible causes of elevated enzymes and an enlarged liver: medication toxicity, alcohol, fatty liver disease, hepatitis, cirrhosis, and other liver diseases such as Wilson's disease. The cause has not been determined.
- Labs drawn today, including liver enzymes and a few other labs.
- Liver ultrasound, hopefully within two weeks. Radiology scheduling will call this afternoon. It can be canceled if the blood work looks good.
- Refrain from drinking any alcohol.
- The doctor will contact the patient with results and determine next steps.

3. Medication review. The doctor noted Crestor can cause liver toxicity and that alternatives may be worth discussing. The doctor recommended the patient call his PCP, who manages his blood pressure and cholesterol. The patient plans to call this afternoon.

Follow-up: Return in four weeks to review the fiber supplement, constipation, and test results, and to decide whether further liver testing is needed. Schedule at checkout.

Bobby is a patient with right shoulder pain for a few weeks. He was sore all over for a couple of days afterward, but the right shoulder has stayed sore and has not gone away. The right is his dominant arm. The patient thinks it could be bursitis. He had prior problems with the same shoulder from an injury playing baseball when younger and has always had some minor issues.

He says the pain does not feel like it is in the rotator cuff. It is more on the outside of the shoulder and is tender on the outside when he raises his arm. He reports no restriction in movement. Pain occurs with movement and he does not notice it when sitting still. It bothers him a little at night because he sleeps on that side. He has been taking Advil and icing, which helps a little and dulls the pain, but the shoulder is still sore to touch. He reports no numbness in the arm or hands.

He also reports that both feet are very sore and stiff, including the ankle joints, which he attributes to a lot of yard work. His wife thinks he does not drink enough water, and he says this could be a factor but he does not know. He has been elevating and icing the feet, which helps a little. He did not identify a specific injury.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever noted on vitals.
Musculoskeletal: Right shoulder pain with movement, mild nighttime discomfort, no restriction in arm movement per patient. Bilateral foot and ankle soreness and stiffness.

Right shoulder x-ray, reviewed by the doctor: no fracture.

- Order MRI of the shoulder given the prior problems with this shoulder, to make sure nothing else is going on.

The patient agreed. The patient's wife thinks inadequate water intake may contribute, but this was not confirmed.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Michelle King is a 39-year-old woman (DOB 01/05/1986, MRN q27631) with a past medical history of anxiety and seasonal allergies. She presents with acid reflux. She has had reflux since about age 12, and it has worsened over the past few years. She describes burning in the chest and throat. She currently takes omeprazole 40 mg twice daily and has been on it for about a year. Some days she is fine, but on other days symptoms are really bad. She feels the omeprazole has helped because of the good days. She previously took omeprazole together with ranitidine, which helped. She has taken no other medications for this.

Triggers: she identifies stress and food choices. Spicy foods bother her and she tries to limit them. Even soda sometimes triggers symptoms. Tomato-based and citrus products sometimes trigger symptoms, but she still eats them. She has not completely cut out these foods.

She denies difficulty swallowing, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, constipation, diarrhea, and rectal bleeding. Weight has been pretty stable. Appetite has been decreased for the past two months, and she has been under a lot of work stress (she is a paralegal).

Family history: maternal grandmother had esophageal cancer. Her mother had acid reflux-type issues and took a medication that coats the stomach lining.

She thinks she may have had an upper endoscopy when she was younger, but none in the last 10 years.

Surgical history: abdominal surgery at about 1 month of age. Her mother told her that her intestines were twisted.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Gastrointestinal: Positive for chest and throat burning and decreased appetite for 2 months. Negative for dysphagia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, bowel habit changes, constipation, diarrhea, and rectal bleeding.
Constitutional: Weight stable.
Psychiatric: Reports significant work stress; stress and anxiety are big problems for her.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
The doctor stated the exam was normal per the new patient template, except for well-healed abdominal surgical scars. Heart and lungs were to be listened to.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Several-year history of GERD, with recent poor control (ongoing heartburn) on omeprazole 40 mg twice daily. Dr. Phillips suspects she likely has GERD with an underlying functional etiology as well. Reassuring features are no unintentional weight loss and no dysphagia. Dr. Phillips mentioned early in the visit that a hiatal hernia might be present but said he was not sure.

Plan:
1. Diet: Avoid trigger foods (spicy foods, carbonated and caffeinated beverages, citrus, tomato-based foods). The patient agreed to do better with this.
2. Stress: Address stress as a trigger, as it may help the GERD.
3. Medication: Switch omeprazole to Nexium 40 mg twice daily. The prescription will be sent to her pharmacy on file. The patient agreed.
4. Procedure: Upper endoscopy (EGD) is recommended to look for potential causes of GERD. It would be done under sedation, with a small camera passed through the mouth, throat, and stomach into the small intestine. The doctor will look for ulcers or precancerous or cancerous conditions and can take biopsies if anything is seen. The patient wants to schedule it today and will do so at the checkout desk.
5. Contingency: If the EGD is normal and symptoms persist despite a trial of Nexium, consider a trial of Protonix and obtain a pH-impedance study. This would rule out abnormal acid reflux exposure and distinguish between a functional etiology and hypersensitivity.
6. Follow-up: Office visit after the EGD to discuss results and her response to the dietary, stress, and medication changes. She should call the office if anything changes or problems arise before the EGD and follow-up.

Yearly follow-up for asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergy.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Emily Hernandez is a 20-year-old female (DOB March 26, 2001) seen for yearly follow-up of asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergy. Her last office visit was in April 2020, and the most recent contact was a telemedicine visit a little over a year ago. Written consent was obtained today to use DAX for documentation.

Asthma: Due to an insurance change she was switched from Symbicort to Wixela 250/50, which she currently uses and says is working well. She is prescribed one puff twice daily, but she has been taking it less because she hopes to enlist in the military in early spring 2022 (in about 6-7 months). She must meet a fitness level without an inhaler, and fitness tests are done without inhaler use that day. She reports using it 3-4 days per week as one puff morning and night, and once daily (morning or night) on the other days. She feels this is working okay and some days feels she does not need it. She rarely uses albuterol, only before strenuous exercise such as a run as prevention. She has no problems with walking or grocery shopping. The patient mentioned that her exertional symptoms might be vocal cord dysfunction but said she is not sure. No urgent care or ER visits for breathing in the past year and no prednisone use. She reports that over the past year she got into vaping and smoking, is trying to quit, and now uses only a little; she thinks this might have an effect. She has a nebulizer but has not used it in a long time (last for bronchitis, and a few times as a child) and needs no refills. Pharmacy is Kaiser Permanente Broadway. Asthma Control Test (ACT) score is 21.

Allergic rhinitis: She uses Zyrtec over the counter, mostly in spring and fall, and as needed in summer. She does not take it daily but takes it on days she will be outside, about three days a week for work. It works great.

Food allergy: Known peanut allergy. Last year she developed hives after touching a car with many peanuts in it while working at Enterprise Rent-A-Car. Since then she wears long sleeves and changes gloves each time and has had no reactions. She notes airplanes serve peanuts. She carries an EpiPen. She has previously had tree nut testing. She recalls eating almonds without a reaction soon after a discussion that she might no longer be allergic to tree nuts, but she tends to avoid all tree nuts. The doctor noted that avoiding both is common.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Rare exertional use of albuterol; no urgent care or ER visits for breathing. Allergic: Seasonal allergy symptoms controlled with Zyrtec; hives with peanut contact last year, none since. Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Ears: Good, with a little wax on both sides.
Mouth: Good.
Nose: Good.
Lungs: Sound terrific.
Heart: Examined with the patient breathing quietly; doctor said "very good."

RESULTS
Spirometry done today: about the same as a couple of years ago and actually a little better. The doctor noted that the last test, in 2019, was done during a smoky wildfire period, which the doctor said explains the lower numbers then.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Asthma: Breathing test is stable to slightly improved, and ACT is 21. The doctor discussed two options. Option 1 is to continue Wixela, used off-label once daily. Option 2 is to step back to a single-medication inhaler, Alvesco, which Kaiser covers. The patient chose Alvesco. Plan:
- Start Alvesco 80 mcg, two puffs twice daily, to be sent to Kaiser Permanente Broadway.
- Keep the Wixela aside and do not throw it away in case Alvesco does not work well.
- Renew albuterol as needed.
- The doctor said newer guidelines suggest possibly using these inhalers only when ill or during smoke season, and that it might be possible to step back to that later. Pulling back too much would be indicated by getting sick or having issues every month.
- Repeat spirometry in four months to document control, since the military sometimes requires documentation of breathing tests.
- Encouraged to continue trying to quit smoking and vaping (patient said she is trying to quit).
2. Allergic rhinitis: Continue Zyrtec 10 mg as needed, over the counter.
3. Peanut allergy: Continue avoiding peanuts and tree nuts. Refill EpiPen.
Follow-up in four months with ACT and spirometry, sooner if needed. Follow-up visit 25 minutes.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

He noticed the tingling and numbness more once the fractures healed. Both hands have worsened over the last month. The right is worse, and his right wrist was in worse shape at the time of the fracture. He wears a splint on the right wrist, and sometimes on the left as well. The splint helps.

The symptoms are mainly soreness, and sometimes the hands throb. They feel weaker, especially with use. He denies loss of sensation but says the hands may be less sensitive than they should be, though he can still feel. He also reports mild neck stiffness. He hit his head in the accident and was told it was a contusion. He was given nerve pain medication but has not been taking it as prescribed.

Constitutional: fatigue and weight gain.
Eyes: floaters.
Cardiovascular: shortness of breath and leg swelling.
GI: excessive appetite and bloating.
Endocrine: always hungry.
Skin: nail bed changes, dryness, itching.
Musculoskeletal: gout and muscle pain. Also mild neck stiffness (per HPI).
Neurologic: numbness and tingling in both hands (per HPI).

- Sensation is normal except for diminished pin prick sensation in the third and fourth fingers on the right.
- Sensation is decreased in the fourth and fifth fingers on the left.
- Reflexes are 1+ and symmetric in the upper extremities, 2+ at the knees. Toes are downgoing bilaterally.
- Tinel sign is positive at both wrists and both elbows. The patient described a "zing" up the wrist and into the elbow on both sides.
- The rest of the exam is normal.

Not discussed.

Assessment: The doctor's impression is bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. Bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome is also possible. The doctor feels the symptom presentation suggests bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, with the wrist nerves aggravated by past trauma, causing the pain and tingling. The doctor initially wondered about a pinched nerve.

4. If symptoms persist, the doctor said referral to the hand clinic could be considered, possibly for injections or carpal tunnel release surgery. Referral to an orthopedist for the same treatment is also an option.

Low back pain radiating down the left leg, referred by PCP. Pain became markedly worse about one month ago.

He points to the lower back with radiation through the hip and down the left leg. He describes the pain as an "electrical toothache" going down the whole leg. Later in the visit he described it as going to the back, hip, side of the leg, side of the calf, and big toe. He reports his foot drags when he walks and he has been using a cane. He says he cannot tie his shoes, standing makes it very bad, and he has been "bedridden." He wonders whether this might be spinal stenosis (patient's own suggestion).

Pain severity: 6/10 at the visit, since he did not take his medications so the doctor could see him as he is. At worst he rates it 13/10. Later he stated 8/10. Lying down is the only thing that relieves it. Standing, walking, coughing, and sneezing worsen it. Sitting in the waiting area for about 30 minutes worsened symptoms. He reports that his back and both legs feel weak. He heard from a friend that the doctor "burned some nerves" and hopes the doctor can relieve his pain today.

Prior treatment: NSAIDs without relief and some physical therapy (per doctor's statement).

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Vision changes, with trouble in the right eye per the visit referral.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Matthew presents with vision changes. He reports difficulty adjusting to dark, dim environments, especially when eating out at restaurants in the evening. He thinks it could be cataracts (patient's opinion). The technician's notes document decreased vision when reading, especially in dark places, and that straight lines such as door frames look crooked. He states the symptoms have been present "a little while" and have probably worsened over the last 3 to 4 months. The straight dark grooves in the paneling in his office always look wavy to him.

He smokes about a pack a day. He has tried hypnosis, lozenges, and nicotine gum and gets close to quitting, but relapses, for example by buying a cigarette when out one evening without his wife.

He has a history of high blood pressure. He has not taken his blood pressure pill for a while; the bottle is in a cupboard corner and he says he can't remember to take it. Whether he checks his blood pressure at home was asked but not answered.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Eyes: Decreased vision when reading and in dim light, distorted (crooked/wavy) straight lines, worsening over 3 to 4 months.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Eyes, anterior segment: Posterior chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes.
Right eye: Cornea clear. No NVI. Cup-to-disc ratio 0.2. Retina attached 360 degrees with no holes or tears. RPE changes in the fovea. Posterior segment shows drusen in the macula, retinal thickening, subretinal fluid, exudate accumulation, and hemorrhage.
Left eye: Cornea clear. No NVI. Cup-to-disc ratio 0.3. RPE changes in the fovea. No hemorrhage or subretinal fluid. Retina attached.

RESULTS
OCT: Drusen deposits under the RPE, subretinal fluid accumulation, and a choroidal neovascular membrane.
Fluorescein angiography: Focal area of leakage in the right eye, consistent with neovascular age-related macular degeneration.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration, right eye. The doctor states the exam and diagnostic tests are consistent with this diagnosis. The doctor explained that it has advanced to a stage that usually leads to more severe vision loss. Abnormal vessels grow beneath the retina and leak fluid and blood, creating a central blind spot. The doctor described it as the most common cause of severe vision loss.
- Monthly intravitreal Lucentis injections after numbing the eye. The patient was told he should not feel pain from the injection.
- The doctor said injections over time can slow the rate of vision decline and may even stop it, though a small amount of vision loss may still occur. This is the best chance of maintaining vision.
- The first injection will be done today. The nurse will prep the patient.
- The patient had no questions and asked only that the injection not hurt much.

2. Tobacco use, about 1 pack per day. The doctor advised cutting back or quitting altogether. Prior attempts included hypnosis, lozenges, and gum.

3. Hypertension with medication nonadherence. The doctor advised taking the blood pressure medication as prescribed, starting today. The doctor suggested placing the pill bottle on the counter as a reminder.

Follow-up for adult hydrocephalus, first visit after shunt surgery on August 1, 2020.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Watson is an 86-year-old male (DOB 04/12/1934) followed since May 2020, when he first presented with eight to ten years of progressive gait impairment, cognitive impairment, and decreased bladder control. The diagnosis of adult hydrocephalus was established with a spinal catheter protocol in June 2020. He underwent shunt surgery on August 1, 2020, with placement of a Medtronic Strata programmable shunt in a ventriculoperitoneal configuration, programmed at level 2.0. He is accompanied by his daughter, Theresa.

Since surgery (about three months), he has not been sick or hospitalized per his daughter. She reports he has been doing much better.

Gait: Per his daughter, walking has improved. He can now walk to the dining room without difficulty, which he could not do before surgery. He still has times when he needs help.

Bladder: Per his daughter, bladder control improved somewhat after surgery but has since leveled off. He wears diapers. No sores from the diaper and no decreased or painful urination.

Cognition: The patient feels he is better and no longer feels lost when talking to someone. His daughter relayed that his other daughter, Hannah, said she feels she can have a normal conversation with him again. The doctor commented that a vitamin B12 deficiency might be a factor but stated he was not sure.

He denies headaches, pain at the shunt site, and abdominal pain.

The patient asked whether he will be able to drive again. He said he does not like to burden anyone when he needs to run to the store but knows he needs to be safe.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Impaired ability to carry out daily functions. Negative for fever or unintentional weight loss.
GU: Urinary incontinence, wears a diaper. Negative for genital sores, decreased or painful urination.
Neurological: Continued walking impairment and cognitive impairment. Negative for headaches, recent falls, or hallucinations.
Psychiatric: Negative for depression, excessive worrying, or mood swings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 124/80, HR 64, RR 18, weight 174 lb, pain 0/10.
General: Pleasant and cooperative, converses easily, though his daughter adds some details.
Shunt site: Clean, dry, and intact. Setting confirmed at 2.
Cognition: Tested for recent and remote memory, attention span, concentration, and fund of knowledge. MMSE 26/30 with spelling and 25/30 with calculations. He recalled two of three memory words with cuing and the third with multiple choice. At the initial test he scored 24/30 with spelling and 23/30 with calculations, and could not recall any memory words with cuing and only one with multiple choice.
Gait (Tinetti, no assistive device): Gait score 6 to 8/12, balance score 12/16, total 18 to 20/28. Initial total was 15 to 17/28.
Cranial nerves: Pupils equal. EOMs intact. Face symmetric. No dysarthria.
Motor: Normal bulk and strength.
Coordination: Slow on finger-to-nose.

RESULTS
CT head 10/15/2020: Frontal horn span at the level of the foramen of Monro 4.6 cm. Third ventricular contour flat with a span of 10 mm. By the doctor's own reading, there is a tiny amount of blood in the right frontal region with a tiny subdural collection. This was not noted by the radiologist, who stated no extra-axial fluid collections. Substantial small vessel ischemic change is also present. (During the visit the doctor described the collection as right parietal.)

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diagnoses: Adult hydrocephalus, gait impairment, urinary incontinence and urgency, and cognitive impairment.

The patient has improved in gait, cognition, and, to a degree, bladder control since shunt surgery. The doctor believes there is a tiny blood/fluid collection on CT but does not believe it is causing symptoms. It was not documented by the radiologist. The patient was told there is nothing to worry about.

Plan:
- Leave the shunt setting unchanged for another two to three months.
- Return in three months. Appointment to be scheduled at the front desk.
- Driving: The doctor feels it is unlikely that his movement speed will improve enough to pass a driver safety evaluation at this point. Some patients improve over nine to 12 months, and the doctor said this could be him. If he improves, the doctor would be happy to recommend evaluation. The patient may enroll in a driver safety program without a recommendation, and improvement will continue to be monitored.
- The doctor is very pleased with his improvement and expects continued improvement at the next visit.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left shoulder pain for a few weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Betty is a patient who reports left shoulder pain for the past few weeks. She wonders whether it might be bursitis (patient's own speculation). She cannot identify a specific onset activity but describes herself as very active and has been renovating her basement. She denies any trauma, including falls or hitting the shoulder. She has had occasional aches and pains in the past that were managed with Tylenol, but no prior pain specifically in this shoulder was described beyond that. The pain is isolated to the left shoulder.

Reaching for or lifting objects causes significant pain, and she does not attempt to raise her arm overhead because of pain. The pain is constant. It worsens with pressure, such as lying on the left side. She is a side sleeper and has difficulty sleeping because of this. The pain is present when lying on her back as well, but increases when she lies directly on the shoulder.

She takes two extra-strength Tylenol every 6 to 8 hours, which takes the edge off. Pain is about 7/10 without Tylenol and 2-3/10 with Tylenol. She denies numbness or tingling in the arm or hand.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Left shoulder pain with limited use of the arm, as above.
Neurological: Denies numbness or tingling in the arm or hand.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Reviewed by the doctor; reported as good.
Left shoulder: Limited active and passive range of motion. Tenderness over the greater tuberosity of the humerus. No tenderness at the sternoclavicular or clavicular joints.
Hand grip: Good bilaterally.
Neurovascular, left arm: Capillary refill brisk (less than 3 seconds). Motor and sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
X-ray of the left shoulder (reviewed by the doctor): No fracture or bony abnormality seen.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left shoulder pain: The doctor believes symptoms are most likely due to rotator cuff tendinopathy, meaning injury to the tendons of the shoulder muscles.
- Order MRI of the left shoulder to make sure nothing else is going on.
- Refer to physical therapy for approximately 6 to 8 weeks.
- Continue Tylenol as needed.
- If symptoms do not improve, the doctor said a steroid injection of the left shoulder could be considered, which could hopefully provide relief.
- The patient asked whether the pain will ever go away. The doctor said he believes it will and that many of his patients do well with PT, so a conservative approach will be started first.
- Follow-up in about two weeks. The nurse will provide paperwork.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
New patient visit for hypertension and palpitations. Recent emergency room visit for high blood pressure and palpitations.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jordan Roberts is a 49-year-old man (DOB 3/2/1972) with hypertension and palpitations. He was seen in the emergency room, which he believes was in March, for high blood pressure and palpitations. The patient reports that on that day he had a few cups of coffee and no breakfast, and he thinks it was probably more of a panic attack than anything else. The doctor wondered whether it might have been low blood sugar. The patient has not felt the palpitations again since.

He reports blood pressure problems since he was young, and a family history of high blood pressure in many relatives. He thought it was improving. A new primary doctor started a new medication about a month ago, a combination pill he described as "40-25," confirmed in the chart as Benicar HCT (contains hydrochlorothiazide). He is also still taking amlodipine 10 mg daily.

He checks his blood pressure at home every morning on getting up. Recent readings are about 146 to 155. He is not yet in the 120s. He is trying to reduce his salt intake and feels he is doing well with it. He tries to walk on the treadmill when he can.

Potassium one week ago was 4.0 and has not been rechecked since.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: No recurrence of palpitations since the emergency room visit.
Gastrointestinal: No abdominal tenderness on palpation.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart and lungs sound good.
Abdomen: Patient denied tenderness with palpation anywhere.
Extremities: Ankles and feet examined for swelling; all looked good.

RESULTS
Potassium one week ago: 4.0.
The doctor requested that the thyroid profile from March 1, 2021 be copied forward; no values were given in the transcript.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Resistant hypertension. The patient is on three medications at maximum doses (amlodipine 10 mg, and Benicar HCT with hydrochlorothiazide) and blood pressure remains above goal. The doctor explained that some people have resistant hypertension driven by another cause, often hormonal, and mentioned parathyroid levels or adrenal overproduction of aldosterone (hyperaldosteronism) as possibilities. No cause has been established.
- Start spironolactone, which the doctor said is very effective at lowering aldosterone and blood pressure. The patient agreed to try it.
- Risks discussed with the patient: electrolyte disturbance and dehydration (maintain hydration; dizziness on standing suggests dehydration), rarely high potassium (starting potassium of 4 gives room), low sodium when combined with hydrochlorothiazide (this does not mean he should eat more salt), dizziness, and gynecomastia in about 1 in 100 men (if chest tenderness or breast enlargement occurs, stop the medication and notify the doctor). The patient said he will report this if it happens.
- Metabolic panel and blood pressure check in two weeks, with follow-up visit in two weeks.
- If not controlled on spironolactone, refer to the resistant hypertension clinic to look for secondary causes and consider procedure-based options such as renal denervation (shown to lower blood pressure by about 10 points; carries risks and not everyone is a candidate). To be decided later.
- The doctor noted the next medication would be carvedilol, which he tries to avoid because of the potential for erectile dysfunction. He discussed this with the patient.
- Counseling: the doctor provided DASH eating plan information. Keep salt under 2000 mg per day (recommendation is 1500 mg), increase potassium, and stay active. Walking on the treadmill about 30 minutes most days could lower blood pressure by 7 to 10 points. The doctor recommended the American Heart Association website heart.org. He explained that uncontrolled hypertension at a young age can lead to an enlarged heart, heart failure, kidney failure, and stroke. The patient understood.

2. Palpitations and recent ER visit. These have not recurred. The patient thinks it was likely a panic attack related to caffeine and skipping breakfast. The doctor wondered about low blood sugar. No further workup was discussed.

Left back pain, with the patient suspecting a kidney stone. Follow-up of hypertension and diabetes.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Linda has a past medical history of hypertension and diabetes. She presents with about 3 days of pain in the left back that has since traveled lower, toward the groin. The pain is constant, and she cannot get comfortable. She reports that she has not passed a stone yet. She is able to urinate and started seeing blood in her urine this morning. She has had some chills but no fever. She feels a little nauseous and cannot eat because of the pain. The patient said it might be a kidney infection but that she is not sure. She believes this is her third kidney stone episode, and she has not had one in a while. Previous stones took about 3 to 4 days to pass. Today is day 3. She has taken Tylenol and some ibuprofen without much relief. She noted that she was told to be careful with ibuprofen because of her blood pressure, but she has used it because of the pain.

Hypertension: She takes Norvasc 2.5 mg. She obtained a home blood pressure cuff but has not been consistent about using it. Her systolic readings are usually in the 130s, sometimes in the 140s, and once reached about 150. Diastolic readings are 70 to 80. At diagnosis her systolic pressure was in the 180s. She is trying to limit salt to about 2300 mg per day but admits she likes french fries. She said help with her diet would be useful.

Diabetes: Her last A1c was 7.3. She takes metformin 500 mg and reports taking it every day. She checks her blood sugar before meals daily, and readings are in the low 100s. A glucose test a couple of months ago was around 300.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Chills. No fever. Poor appetite due to pain.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain.
Gastrointestinal: Nausea. No abdominal pain.
Genitourinary: Hematuria this morning. Able to urinate. Pain radiating from the back toward the groin.
Musculoskeletal: Left back pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiovascular: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously known.
Respiratory: Lungs clear bilaterally. No crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen: Tenderness to palpation. No rebound or guarding.
Back/Flank: CVA tenderness on the right flank per the doctor's statement. Back palpation was painful.
Vitals: Blood pressure was described as a little high today, which the doctor attributed to pain.

RESULTS
No results from today's visit. Previously reviewed: A1c 7.3 at the last visit. Glucose about 300 a couple of months ago.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Kidney stone, recurrent (third episode). Based on her history and exam, the doctor believes she has a kidney stone and that the CVA tenderness indicates some inflammation around the kidney.
- Oxycodone 5 mg every 6 to 8 hours as needed for pain.
- Continue Tylenol for breakthrough pain.
- Push fluids.
- Strain urine to check for passage of the stone.
- Refer to urology, to be seen even if the stone passes, because of recurrent stones and to help prevent future episodes.

2. Hypertension. Blood pressures at home are acceptable per the doctor. Continue Norvasc 2.5 mg with no changes. Encourage regular home blood pressure monitoring and sodium reduction to about 2300 mg per day.

3. Diabetes. Continue metformin 500 mg. Refer to a dietitian for diet help. The doctor hopes that with dietary changes she may eventually come off both medications.

The patient agreed with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hospital follow-up after an acute on chronic congestive heart failure exacerbation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is an 82-year-old male with a past medical history of hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. He presents for follow-up after a hospitalization for heart failure exacerbation.

Before admission, he was trying to watch his diet but noticed ankle swelling. One day he became very short of breath and called 911. Paramedics placed him on a breathing mask. In the ER he was told his blood pressure was very high; the doctor noted it was 200/90 on chart review. He admits to missing a dose or two of his medications at times, though he tries to take them. He acknowledges dietary slips, including pizza, cheese, and chicken wings at weekend parties with friends.

In the hospital for a couple of days, he received a medicine that made him urinate a lot, then a water pill through an IV. He believes his blood pressure medications were changed. He feels much better now. Since discharge he reports following his diet and taking his medications because he does not want to return to the hospital. He bought a home blood pressure cuff last week, checks it about every other day, and reports his readings have been very good. He denies shortness of breath, trouble sleeping, and chest pain since returning home. He is able to move around without trouble and takes a good afternoon nap.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Feels good; no sleep problems.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain. Ankle swelling before admission.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath currently.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 128/72, heart rate 79, respiratory rate 26 (doctor thought this was probably due to talking), O2 saturation 99%. Vital signs otherwise look good in general.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously heard and stable.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram (reviewed by doctor): preserved EF of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure: The doctor stated it sounds like this was caused by dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension.
- Continue Bumex 2 mg daily.
- Continue to watch diet and avoid salty foods; cut back on pizza and chicken wings.
- Weigh daily; call if he gains about 3 pounds in 2 days.
- Refer to a nutritionist for education on what foods he can eat.
- Continue monitoring the stable systolic murmur.
- The trace edema is expected to be helped by the water pill.

2. Hypertension: Blood pressure today is 128/72.
- Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily and Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
- Take medications consistently.
- Order renal artery ultrasound to ensure no secondary causes are being missed.

3. Chronic kidney disease: Order additional labs to make sure he tolerates this regimen.

Follow-up in 3 months. The patient had no further questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Uncontrolled high blood pressure despite medication; referred by PCP for evaluation, also noted abnormal kidney-related finding on recent blood work.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Virginia started seeing a new PCP last year. The PCP has made several medication changes and added two medications after noting high blood pressure. The patient reports she was previously not taking her medications consistently but is now taking them reliably. Blood pressure remains difficult to control. The PCP referred her to this clinic, and the patient states the PCP mentioned something about her kidneys on the last blood work.

Most days she feels fine and remains busy at work. She states she can tell when her blood pressure is high. She checks her blood pressure at home a few times a week with an electronic arm cuff. Readings have been rising, with one recently as high as 170/90. She called her PCP, who increased her medications again. She notes that CVS no longer has a blood pressure station since the pandemic; the doctor believed the one on Main Street may have brought it back.

Diet: She admits her diet could be better. She eats a lot of pizza, wings, and subs, especially during football season, and is trying to cut down, particularly on days without games.

Medications: amlodipine (Norvasc) 10 mg daily and carvedilol 25 mg twice daily. She was previously on lisinopril, which was changed with the adjustments. She takes NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin, Aleve) occasionally for knee or back pain, not daily.

Alcohol: A couple of beers during the week and one or two on the weekends.

Family history: Both parents have high blood pressure, and one had kidney disease.

During the visit the doctor commented that sleep apnea might be a possibility but stated he was not sure.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Feels fine most days.
Neurologic: Mild headaches only when blood pressure is very high; no regular headaches.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain. Slight lower extremity swelling after prolonged time on her feet, otherwise none.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath, including with exertion.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 169/74, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 98%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Lungs: Clear.
Cardiovascular: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur heard; doctor stated this needs a closer look.
Extremities: 1+ pitting edema bilaterally.

RESULTS
No results were reviewed during the visit. The patient reported the PCP noted something about her kidneys on recent blood work; no values were discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Uncontrolled hypertension. The doctor stated the cause is often multifactorial and that medications may need to be changed. He plans to order tests to look for a specific cause before making further medication changes.
- Renal artery ultrasound to look for narrowing of the kidney blood vessels.
- Morning aldosterone level, renin level, and 24-hour urine collection to evaluate for adrenal problems.
- Start doxazosin (Cardura) 4 mg once daily.
- Decrease alcohol to one or two drinks per week.
- Decrease salt intake substantially; referral to a nutritionist.
- Stop NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin); use only Tylenol for pain.
- Record all home blood pressures over the next three weeks, taking them at the same time each day, and bring the record to the visit.
- Return in 3 weeks.
- The doctor will speak with the PCP to coordinate care.

2. Systolic ejection murmur (2/6), newly noted on exam. The doctor said it needs an extra look; no specific workup was specified.

3. Bilateral 1+ pitting edema noted on exam; no specific plan discussed.

The patient had no questions, expressed hope that the plan will work, and agreed with it.
